key_findings.finding: The infusion day itself is largely passive and sedating, not active: pre-meds (IV steroids + Benadryl + anti-nausea) make patients wired for the first 1-2 hours, then they doze through most of a 6-8 hour infusion, and need to be driven home.
key_findings.evidence: "On chemo day, I received IV steroids through my port, along with Benadryl and anti-nausea drugs. Initially, I was wide awake for the first hour or two of chemo due to the steroids. Then, I drifted into a deep nap for a few hours." Another: "loaded up with Benadryl and mostly doze for the next 6 hours."

key_findings.finding: A chemo cycle has a predictable shape: the infusion day and day 1-2 are buffered by steroids, the crash hits around days 4-5 when steroids wear off but sickness remains, then gradual recovery to a near-normal final week before the next cycle.
key_findings.evidence: TCHP patient Irishgirl16: "Days 4 and 5 were the worst for me, the steroids had worn off but the sickness was there then." General guidance: "The worst days after a chemotherapy infusion tend to be days 3-5. This often coincides with stopping the corticosteroids."

key_findings.finding: On a take-home-pump regimen (e.g. FOLFOX-style), the week splits into a non-functional block (infusion day + ~46h pump = Mon-Wed) and a single usable week, with Thursday a recovering-but-rough day.
key_findings.evidence: Kris (stomach cancer): infusion "six to eight hours"; take-home "chemo purse, which runs for 46 additional hours. So all day Tuesday and most of Wednesday"; "you don't really feel that great on Thursday. I typically go to work on Thursday, but you don't feel that good"; "Then you just have the next week, where you can do something."

key_findings.finding: Morning fatigue and evening fatigue are statistically DISTINCT phenomena with different triggers, meaning the same patient can have a workable morning and a wiped-out evening (or vice versa) - the day is not uniformly tired.
key_findings.evidence: Miaskowski 582-patient study: morning fatigue classes Low 31.8% / High 51.4% / Very High 16.8%; evening fatigue Moderate 20.0% / High 21.8% / Very High 58.2%. "a higher number of comorbid conditions was associated with more severe morning fatigue, whereas caring for children at home was associated with more severe evening fatigue."

key_findings.finding: Evening fatigue is far more prevalent and persistent than morning fatigue: ~80% of patients hit clinically meaningful evening fatigue vs ~67% morning, and morning fatigue oscillates with the treatment cycle (peaks weeks 1 and 3) while evening fatigue stays elevated throughout.
key_findings.evidence: "80% of the patients in this study experienced clinically meaningful levels of evening fatigue" vs 67% for morning fatigue. Morning fatigue showed "oscillating pattern with peaks at weeks 1 and 3 post-treatment"; evening fatigue "remained persistently elevated."

key_findings.finding: Within a single day, fatigue tends to rise as the day progresses and peaks at bedtime rather than mid-afternoon - the morning is the relatively good window, and anxious mood and difficulty thinking specifically worsen in the afternoon/evening.
key_findings.evidence: "within-day fluctuations in fatigue were lowest during mid-morning or early afternoon, and increased as the day progressed, peaking at bedtime." EMA breast cancer study: "Afternoon and evening symptoms of anxious mood increased slightly" and evening difficulty thinking worsened (p=0.01); "Morning active mood improved significantly (p<0.01)."

key_findings.finding: The mid-morning is the recommended and lived 'good window' for getting things done; patients and clinicians schedule demanding tasks then and plan a short early-afternoon nap, treating the afternoon dip as a known event.
key_findings.evidence: "schedule the most demanding tasks—appointments, paperwork, or chores—when feeling most alert, usually mid-morning." Naps "should be limited to 20-30 minutes and scheduled early in the afternoon to avoid disrupting nighttime rest."

key_findings.finding: Steroid-driven insomnia is a named, dreaded feature of the early-cycle nights: roughly 45% of dexamethasone-treated patients report moderate-severe insomnia, and patients name days 1-2 as their worst specifically because steroids wreck their sleep, not because of nausea.
key_findings.evidence: "Patients receiving dexamethasone reported moderate–severe problems with insomnia (45%), in the week following chemotherapy." SusanHB: "My worst days are days 1 and 2, mainly because my sleep is impacted by the steroids."

key_findings.finding: Fragmented night sleep with a 3-4 hour ceiling and early-morning waking is common; about half of patients report frequent night awakenings and early awakenings, and many can paradoxically sleep better in the day than at night.
key_findings.evidence: "frequent night awakenings (49%–56%)... early awakenings (49%–65%)"; "nearly 80% of cancer patients report sleep problems." And: patients "report altered diurnal rhythms, the ability to sleep better during the day, or being able to sleep for only 3 or 4 h before awakening."

key_findings.finding: The night after infusion can be punctuated by clockwork vomiting episodes (midnight and 3am) - acute nausea peaks 5-6 hours post-infusion and delayed nausea peaks 48-72h, with a subset peaking on day 3.
key_findings.evidence: Dutch diary: "om 12 uur en 3 uur liggen kotsen, voelde me echt hondsberoerd" (vomited at midnight and 3 AM, felt absolutely terrible). Clinical: acute nausea "maximal intensity after 5–6 hours"; delayed nausea "peaking at 48-72 hours... sometimes peaking on day 3."

key_findings.finding: On crash days the body fails at basic vertical movement: stairs and short walks to the kitchen become the limiting activity, and the day collapses to bed/couch with brief upright windows.
key_findings.evidence: Dutch diary: "zelfs de trap op lopen ging bijna niet" (could barely walk up the stairs); "misselijk, gevoel van zware griep, krachtverlies" (nauseous, feeling of heavy flu, loss of strength). Gary (Jersey): "half an hour ago I made the slow and short walk to the kitchen to sort a cuppa" was notable effort.

key_findings.finding: Upright social/active windows are short and rationed - patients can manage roughly 90-minute bouts before needing to lie down, and one diarist's day structure was an afternoon sleep block plus the night.
key_findings.evidence: Gary (Jersey, UK): activity windows of "90 minute catch-ups" with visitors before needing rest; sleep "Usually 1pm to 5pm/6pm and then overnight from 8pm to 5am."

key_findings.finding: The post-infusion days produce a cyclical nausea-and-immobility loop where eating shrinks to a handful of bland items and any errand requires being dragged through it; the day is organized around managing the puke-or-feel-like-puking baseline.
key_findings.evidence: Sylvia Soo (Canada): "When I wasn't puking, I felt like puking. When I didn't feel like puking, it was extremely hard to muster enough energy to move." Day after: "only managed to eat about eight crackers"; described self as "a fish whose stomach had been gutted out."

key_findings.finding: Cumulative toxicity reshapes the day across cycles: later infusions hit harder, and patients map a 'steroid crash' day (e.g. day 9 on EC, or breathlessness emerging day 5 on docetaxel) that did not exist in early cycles.
key_findings.evidence: Lovely Louis (UK): EC "first 3 days, ie slightly nauseous, headache and aches" but "The steroid crash on day 9 was awful"; docetaxel "I was fine for the first 4 days, then it took my breath away" with days 5-12 "breathless, racing heart, mouth ulcers, diarrhoea."

key_findings.finding: Even when a patient stays functional, the day is re-engineered around symptom timing rather than taken off entirely - flexible scheduling (no early calls, buffer for bad nights) matters more than full days off.
key_findings.evidence: Irishgirl16 (TCHP, 6 cycles): worked from home and "never took a full day off" but avoided early morning calls "to give me a chance to sleep if I had a bad night."

key_findings.finding: Beyond symptoms, the cancer day is heavily consumed by logistics: patients spend a median of ~7 hours/week managing cancer, do at least one care-related home task on 80% of days, and travel/wait time (median 35 min travel; 14% of visits wait >1h) often exceeds time actually receiving care.
key_findings.evidence: "they spent a median of 400 minutes—or nearly seven hours—per week managing their cancer"; "did at least one cancer-related task at home on 80% of study days"; "the median travel time was 35 minutes... 14% of care episodes involved a wait time of more than an hour."

key_findings.finding: Objective actigraphy confirms the lived day shape: lower daytime activity than healthy controls, and during chemo specifically more time awake at night and more activity at night (i.e. the day-night rhythm inverts and flattens as treatment progresses).
key_findings.evidence: "Cancer patients presented lower daytime activity than healthy controls"; "During chemotherapy, patients had lower sleep efficiency, more time awake, and higher activity levels at night." Breast cancer patients show "progressively impaired sleep-wake activity rhythms during chemotherapy."

key_findings.finding: Pre-chemo sleep quality sets the tone for the whole 3-week cycle: patients who slept poorly the night before infusion (~55% of one sample) reported greater fatigue and more anxious mood across the entire cycle, so the night before is a leverage point for the days after.
key_findings.evidence: "Those with poor pre-CT sleep (PSQI ≥5, 55% of sample) reported greater fatigue and 'less calm/more anxious mood' throughout the 3-week cycle"; good pre-chemo sleep showed "a buffering effect against anxious mood in early post-infusion days."

key_findings.finding: Within the NL context, the recovery week is non-linear and explicitly tracked by patients as 'two steps forward': improvement starts a few days post-infusion and feels near-complete by about day 7, when normal activities (drives, jogging attempts) resume.
key_findings.evidence: "Vanaf zaterdag ging het ietsje beter, 2 stapjes vooruit" (from Saturday it got a bit better, two steps forward) after a Tuesday infusion; cycle 4: "Na een week voelde ik me gelukkig weer een stuk beter" (after a week I felt considerably better again), then a jogging attempt with a single song on repeat.

key_findings.finding: Chemo brain compounds the bad hours: up to ~75% of patients have cognitive dysfunction during treatment - word-finding loss, short attention, mental fog - which worsens in the afternoon/evening alongside fatigue and degrades the same windows fatigue already takes.
key_findings.evidence: "up to 75 percent of cancer patients experience some form of cognitive dysfunction during treatment"; symptoms include "struggling to find the right words... short attention span... feeling sluggish, mentally tired or drained." EMA study found evening "difficulty thinking worsened (p=0.01)."

surprises: The day is NOT uniformly tired - morning fatigue and evening fatigue are statistically distinct phenotypes with different causes, and within-day fatigue is lowest mid-morning and peaks at BEDTIME, not mid-afternoon as commonly assumed. The morning is reliably the best window. A daily companion should treat mid-morning as the action window and front-load anything cognitively or physically demanding there.

The infusion day is sedating, not active: patients are wired for 1-2 hours on steroids then sleep through most of a 6-8 hour drip on Benadryl. The hard part is not the chair - it is days 4-5 when the steroid buffer drops out. This decouples 'treatment day' from 'worst day' entirely.

Steroids are a double villain on a delay: they buffer you (you feel deceptively okay days 1-2) AND they cause the insomnia that wrecks the night-before/night-of sleep (~45% moderate-severe insomnia), and then their withdrawal produces a named 'steroid crash' (day 9 on EC, days 4-5 on TCHP). Patients track the crash day as a distinct calendar event.

Pre-infusion sleep quality predicts fatigue and mood for the ENTIRE 3-week cycle, not just the next day. The night before chemo is a high-leverage intervention point that a companion could target days in advance.

Patients already run a sophisticated internal scheduling model - 90-minute upright windows, no early-morning calls, naps capped early afternoon, 'never took a full day off but restructured the day.' The unmet need is less 'tell me what's happening' and more 'help me allocate my rationed good hours and protect them.'

The regimen architecture dictates the week's shape more than the cancer type: a 46-hour take-home pump (FOLFOX-style) carves the week into a dead Mon-Wed block plus one usable week, which is a completely different day-planning problem than a one-shot infusion every 3 weeks.
gaps_or_caveats: Source skew is heavily US, then UK, with two NL/Dutch primary voices (kanker.nl) and one Canadian. I found Dutch diaries with verbatim quotes but did not find NL ecological-momentary or time-use studies; the quantified diurnal/fatigue-class numbers are all US (Miaskowski/MD Anderson cohorts). EU generalizability of the exact percentages is unverified.

Most quantified diurnal data is from breast and mixed solid-tumor cohorts (Miaskowski), not specifically oncology beachhead severe paths; FOLFOX/take-home-pump day shape comes from individual patient narratives (Kris) rather than time-use studies.

True minute-by-minute hour-by-hour reconstructions are scarce in published form; most first-person sources narrate by day ('day 4 was worst') rather than by clock hour. The clock-time texture (midnight/3am vomiting, 1pm-6pm nap block, mid-morning good window) is assembled from several partial sources rather than one continuous validated log.

Several richer first-person sources (Cancer Health 'A Short Day in the Life', LiveStrong chemo diaries, Mayo Connect sleepiness thread, CSN 1:30am thread, a YouTube chemo-weekend vlog) returned 403/404/redirect/empty and could not be fully extracted; their detailed timelines are partially captured only via search-result snippets, not verified primary text.

Anti-emetic regimens have improved markedly, so older studies showing low overall nausea (e.g. the EMA breast cancer cohort) may understate nausea in less-controlled real-world or severe-path settings; conversely some vivid diary accounts may predate current anti-emetic standards. Timing of nausea relative to current prophylaxis should be re-validated for the specific regimens Ditto's oncology users are on.

I did not separately reconstruct the caregiver's day (the care circle), which is core to Ditto's growth thesis; sources noted caregivers average ~8h/day of care but I did not gather hour-by-hour caregiver-day texture in this pass.

key_findings.finding: Steroid (dexamethasone) mood follows a predictable weekly cycle tied to dose day: a 1-2 day high/euphoria, then a crash with irritability and low mood roughly 40 hours later.
key_findings.evidence: "I would take it on Mondays so that I would have high energy for the first few days...crash would come around Wednesday afternoon or Thursday" (Eric Hofacket). Separately, a Beacon column: dosed Wednesday night → dex high Thursday → insomnia Thursday night → crash by Friday afternoon, "about 40 hours after taking the medication."

key_findings.finding: Dex day is named and recognized by families as a behavioral event; the patient becomes hyper-irritable and 'barks orders,' and the crash days bring intense anger, confusion and meanness.
key_findings.evidence: "Dex Day! They knew on Mondays he would come in like a bear barking orders." Caregivers at a seminar: "I want my husband back!" and "I may kill him if the multiple myeloma doesn't kill him first!" A spouse described "the following four days of him coming down from that 'high' and intense anger and confusion and meaness."

key_findings.finding: Dex insomnia is total on the dose night and patients fill the small hours with quiet busywork; sleep debt compounds across 3-4 nights before the crash.
key_findings.evidence: "On Mondays, when I receive 40 mg, I am almost guaranteed not to sleep for the night, maybe for 2 hours at most... I usually read, organize a few papers, pet my dog, and tie up loose ends" (Joseph Schutz). "By the third night, I am crashing" (willow75). Pat: "I would wake up at 4 a.m. the following morning like clock-work."

key_findings.finding: Steroid energy is channeled into compulsive overnight cleaning/organizing; the energy is real but unsustainable and ends in a crash.
key_findings.evidence: Forum reports: "usually on Monday (even though don't sleep Sunday night) all I want to do is clean, wash clothes, change sheets, etc"; patients advised to "organize those photo albums. Clean the garage." Pattern: dex "makes most patients hyper, leading them to go and go and go, only to crash in a few days."

key_findings.finding: The chemo cycle has a recognized emotional/physical low at days 3-5, which coincides with the steroid wearing off; patients then recover and feel almost normal in the third week, just in time to dread the next round.
key_findings.evidence: "Days 4 and 5 were the worst for me, the steroids had worn off but the sickness was there then" (Irishgirl16, UK). Another: nearly three weeks after round 3, "the first they felt almost normal, yet they were absolutely dreading the next treatment." Mood swings/anxiety "most intense...around days 5-10 after the infusion."

key_findings.finding: Night is the single hardest emotional window: when the lights go off and distraction stops, thoughts go straight to cancer and death.
key_findings.evidence: "One of the toughest times I have is when I go to bed at night. After I turn off the lights and am in the dark, my thoughts go immediately to my cancer and possibly dying from it." NPR My Cancer blog: "those dark hours in the night when it can feel like all we have is fear."

key_findings.finding: Scanxiety has a measurable timing envelope: fear of recurrence peaks in roughly the 6 days before a surveillance scan, with the highest worry on results-disclosure day; the night before is reliably the worst.
key_findings.evidence: EMA study: "Fear of cancer recurrence (FCR) peaked in the 6 days before surveillance scans compared to 5 days after receiving results (p<0.001)... highest worry on the day of the appointment when results were disclosed." FightCRC patients: "My anxiety starts up about a week before scans" (Lara Lambert); "The night before is the worst. I usually don't sleep" (Leticia Alvarenga).

key_findings.finding: Scanxiety is experienced as countdown-to-verdict dread, not fear of the scan itself; patients fixate on the waiting interval and put life on hold.
key_findings.evidence: Tweets analyzed: "every 3 months, cancer makes me feel like a death row prisoner hoping for a stay of execution"; "It is only 96 hours, 47 minutes, and 34 seconds"; "I will not be making plans until I know whether I get to have my next 3 months"; "we've entered the 'rip off all my cuticles' phase of scanxiety."

key_findings.finding: Identity loss is acute and recurring: patients describe ceasing to be themselves and becoming 'a patient,' wanting to feel like their own name again rather than a sick body.
key_findings.evidence: Dutch patient Deborah: "Me gewoon even Deborah voelen in plaats van dat zieke, vermoeide hoopje mens" ("Just feel like Deborah for a moment instead of this sick, exhausted heap of a person"). US: "When I became a patient, I felt this identity slipping away. Immediately the focus was on my illness and treatment."

key_findings.finding: Profound daily fatigue is itself an emotional event: it strips dignity and reframes naps from luxury to survival, leaving patients unable to perform trivial acts.
key_findings.evidence: Deborah (NL): "Je staat 'geslooptmoe' op en je gaat meerdere malen per dag 'kapotmoe' naar bed" ("You wake up utterly wrecked and go to bed several times a day completely drained"). Another NL patient: lay watching mindless TV "enkel omdat de afstandsbediening net buiten mijn bereik lag en ik van oververmoeidheid de beweging om dat ding te pakken niet kon maken" (couldn't reach the remote from exhaustion).

key_findings.finding: Numbness and emotional flatness are common; patients function on autopilot, going to appointments and signing forms while feeling 'nothing' and dissociated.
key_findings.evidence: Linda (UK): "I didn't cry. I didn't scream... I felt… nothing. Just numb." "I moved through everything in a fog. I went to appointments, signed forms, listened to doctors... I smiled politely and nodded while inside I felt like I was floating outside my body." Another UK survivor: "I was just numb. I would shuffle about all day."

key_findings.finding: Maternal guilt is concrete and daily: guilt over fatigue stealing afternoons with kids and having to explain 'sad Mommy,' plus grief for an imagined future.
key_findings.evidence: Mother named Morris (NPR): "I felt so guilty at first for how much we were going to have to go through as a family," guilty for "losing afternoons to fatigue after treatments, or having to explain being 'sad Mommy' to her toddler." Another mother: "I was grieving for the loss of the future...that I had in my head."

key_findings.finding: Patients withhold their pain from family specifically to avoid being a burden, choosing to talk to counselors instead of loved ones.
key_findings.evidence: "Many clients tell counselors they appreciate talking with a counselor rather than their friends/family because they 'don't want to burden them' with their painful journey all the time." Dutch sources echo guilt "because others are suffering as a result of your situation."

key_findings.finding: Anger is a real but under-discussed daily emotion; patients need permission to rage and feel betrayed by their own bodies and by recurrence.
key_findings.evidence: LBBC blogger: "I needed someone to allow me the space to rage. I needed someone to scream 'it's not fair' over and over with, cursing our genetics." "That anger, for me, was a gift." "it's infuriating to constantly fear it will find you again."

key_findings.finding: Dark/gallows humor is an active daily coping tool, framed as living in a 'whack-a-mole' where the hammer can fall any time; it bonds the cancer community but can alienate outsiders.
key_findings.evidence: Patients describe living with chronic cancer as "being stuck in the upright position in a whack-a-mole game" where "the hammer could come down at any time." "The jokes make me feel better" (Beth Caldwell). One patient joked to her oncologist "about starting a life of crime and he became upset" - humor not always shared.

key_findings.finding: Moments of normalcy fire during mundane sensory domestic acts (dishes, warm water, family sounds), but are explicitly experienced as fragile 'illusion' over constant disease-awareness.
key_findings.evidence: Metastatic breast cancer blogger: "Sometimes I stand at the sink, hot water running, bubbles rising, dishes clinking together, and for a moment, it feels like life is ordinary again." "beneath the illusion of normalcy lives a constant awareness: I have metastatic breast cancer... ever present in my body, in my thoughts, in the way I move through every day."

key_findings.finding: Daily life is experienced as a continuous, granular loss - especially loss of choice and independence - not a single dramatic event; mornings tend to be the better-functioning window.
key_findings.evidence: Advanced cancer patients (Canada study): "The loss is daily. It is the loss of...choice" (Chris). "For me, just to be able to do a couple of dishes, put my hands in the warm water..." (Jessica). "In the morning I feel better, so it's like a different kind of socialising" (Melissa).

key_findings.finding: Nights are spent in fragmented stages of sleep punctuated by pain and rumination, with hours awake in the dark - a recurring nightly pattern, not a one-off.
key_findings.evidence: Dutch palliative patient (ROAR blog): "'s Nachts lig ik vaak wakker van de pijn of slaap ik in etappes: 2 à 3 uur slapen, minimaal een uur wakker, weer in slaap" ("At night I often lie awake from pain or sleep in stages: 2-3 hours, at least an hour awake, then back to sleep").

key_findings.finding: Physical reminders make forgetting cancer impossible even on calm days; the body itself (scars, port, missing breasts) re-triggers patient identity constantly.
key_findings.evidence: Search-surfaced from CURE 'The Impossibility of Forgetting Cancer': author notes having no breasts, "scars all over their chest and back," and a "little port scar," while wanting to forget and get "back to the business of daily life" - but cannot. (Full article 403-blocked; summary only.)

surprises: The steroid (dexamethasone) emotional cycle is the most precisely-timed and family-disruptive pattern in the entire dataset - families literally name and brace for 'Dex Day,' and the crash hits on a near-clockwork ~40-hour delay (Monday dose → Wednesday/Thursday crash; Wednesday dose → Friday crash). This is a calendar-predictable emotional event an AI companion could anticipate and pre-empt, unlike most cancer emotions.

Scanxiety is quantifiably anticipatory: fear peaks in the ~6 days BEFORE the scan, not after, and the dread is about the waiting verdict rather than the scan procedure ('death row prisoner hoping for a stay of execution'). The intervention window is the pre-scan week and the results-wait, both predictable from a calendar.

Patients describe the worst emotional collapse not at diagnosis but when treatment ENDS ('some women process it when they get the news, but others, like me, face it all when the treatment is done. And that's when it gets hard') - the quiet weeks are harder than the busy ones.

Moments of normalcy are triggered by deeply mundane sensory domestic acts - hands in warm dishwater, a child laughing in the next room - and patients consistently frame them as a fragile 'illusion' rather than relief. The everyday is both the refuge and the reminder.

Patients actively hide distress from their own family to avoid being a burden and prefer a neutral third party - a strong signal that an AI companion's non-judgmental, no-burden availability could fill a real emotional gap that loved ones structurally cannot.
gaps_or_caveats: Reddit (r/cancer, r/CancerFamilySupport) is fully blocked to the search agent, removing one of the richest sources of raw, unfiltered daily verbatims. Findings skew toward curated blogs, foundation patient-story pages, and forums that survive crawling.

Several high-value first-person sources were 403-blocked or paywalled via fetch (CURE Magazine articles, Inspire and Mayo Clinic Connect forums, Tandfonline qualitative study), so some findings rest on search-snippet summaries rather than fully verified full-text quotes - flagged at lower confidence.

Steroid-timing verbatims are overwhelmingly from multiple myeloma patients (weekly oral dex regimens), where the rhythm is most pronounced. The oncology beachhead (e.g. solid tumors with dex as a chemo pre-med) likely shows a similar but cycle-bound pattern; timing detail there is thinner and partly inferred.

Geography skews US, then UK, with a solid NL/Belgium thread (Kanker.nl, Helen Dowling Instituut, Belgian EMA studies). Genuinely Dutch first-person DAILY-texture verbatims with explicit timing are scarcer than US/UK ones - worth deeper NL-language hunting for the local market.

Much first-person writing online is from metastatic/advanced and survivor populations who write publicly; the 'ordinary Tuesday' of someone mid-treatment but not blogging is under-represented and may differ. The explicit 'what do I need emotionally on a normal Tuesday' question is answered more by inference (normalcy triggers, no-burden listening, anticipating predictable bad days) than by patients stating it directly.

Identity-loss and numbness quotes cluster around diagnosis and treatment-end transitions rather than steady-state ordinary weeks; the steady-state ordinary-week emotional texture is best captured by the fatigue, night-rumination, and normalcy-illusion findings.

key_findings.finding: Patients in active systemic therapy spend a median of 400 minutes (6.7 hours) per week on cancer-related tasks, with the top of the range hitting 603 minutes (10+ hours) per week.
key_findings.evidence: Participants spent a median (IQR) of 400 (266-603) minutes per week on cancer-related tasks.
key_findings.geography: US (Univ. of Minnesota + Univ. of Alabama at Birmingham; 60 metastatic breast/advanced ovarian patients, Dec 2023-Sep 2024)

key_findings.finding: More than half of that weekly load is invisible at-home admin: medication management, scheduling appointments, medical bills, symptom monitoring, info-seeking and arranging help/transport take a median 209 min/week (up to 355 min in the top quartile).
key_findings.evidence: At-Home Tasks: Median 209 minutes (IQR: 121-355 minutes/week) ... medications, scheduling, medical bills, symptom management, health monitoring, information-seeking, arranging support.

key_findings.finding: For every 1 hour of actual treatment, patients spend roughly 2 hours traveling and waiting, so the logistics of getting care exceed the care itself.
key_findings.evidence: Participants spent roughly 2 hours on travel/waiting for every 1 hour of direct care ... 'For many patients, the hours spent traveling, waiting, or managing care at home far exceed the time spent in actual treatment.' (co-author Helen Parsons)

key_findings.finding: The lead researcher names the load directly: managing cancer is 'like a part-time job' and now there is objective time-tracking data to back what patients have said for years.
key_findings.evidence: 'For years, patients have been telling us that managing cancer is like a part-time job—and now we have the objective data to support that.' (lead author Rachel Vogel)

key_findings.finding: Cancer admin disrupts ordinary daily life on most days: 35% of patients reported tasks interfered with self-care, chores, work or socializing on more than half of study days.
key_findings.evidence: 35% of participants (21 of 60) reported cancer tasks disrupted daily activities—self-care, chores, work, or socializing—on more than 50% of study days.

key_findings.finding: A single bad admin day can swallow four hours across driving, care coordination, and fighting insurance — captured in a patient's own words.
key_findings.evidence: 'Today was a good day. I only spent two hours driving to appointments, another hour coordinating care and a final hour on the phone with insurance.'

key_findings.finding: US insurance prior-authorization is a massive, concentrated time sink that lands on patients and families: when directly involved, 51% lost up to a full business day, 27% lost 2-3 days, and 12% lost a full business week or more per single authorization.
key_findings.evidence: When patients or families got directly involved in authorizations ... 51% lost up to a full business day, 27% lost up to 2-3 business days, and 12% lost a full business week or more to dealing with a single authorization request.

key_findings.finding: Prior authorization is near-universal in US cancer care and mostly pointless friction: 85% faced it, 40% had treatment delayed, yet 95% of requests were eventually approved.
key_findings.evidence: 85% had their insurance companies require prior authorization ... 40% had treatment delayed because of this red tape, despite 95% of authorization requests eventually being approved.

key_findings.finding: Caregivers carry an enormous parallel time load: an estimated 6.1 million US cancer caregivers average 33 hours/week, a quarter exceed 40 hours/week, and intensity peaks at ~66 hours/week in the patient's last year of life.
key_findings.evidence: 6.1 million caregivers of people with cancer are spending, on average, 33 hours per week caregiving ... approximately one-quarter ... spend in excess of 40 hours a week ... 66 hours per week during the patient's last year of life.

key_findings.finding: Childcare is a hidden point of failure: nearly 50% of cancer patients with children rescheduled oncology appointments due to lack of childcare, and 1 in 7 radiotherapy patients missed appointments for childcare reasons.
key_findings.evidence: Nearly 50% of cancer patients with children still rescheduled oncology appointments due to lack of childcare ... One in seven patients on radiotherapy missed appointments for childcare reasons.

key_findings.finding: The childcare safety net is thin and itself overloaded: family and friends supply 80%+ of childcare for parents in treatment, but 90% of those helpers have their own jobs and over half have their own dependent children.
key_findings.evidence: Family and friends account for more than 80% of childcare support systems ... 90% of support networks had their own jobs; over half had dependent children.

key_findings.finding: Medication management is a logistics problem in itself: some cancer patients take up to 20 pills a day and must call the pharmacy 5+ days before running out, juggling standing vs as-needed (anti-nausea) refills.
key_findings.evidence: Cancer treatment usually involves taking a lot of medications ... with some patients taking up to 20 pills a day ... Remember to call 5 or more days before you run out of medications.

key_findings.finding: A Dutch breast cancer patient's diary shows the practical load is family-wide and runs on top of treatment: getting everyone to their appointments, filling stomachs at night, keeping the house presentable, all while coming home exhausted daily.
key_findings.evidence: 'Ik zorg in het dagelijks leven voor mijn mannen. Dat iedereen optijd bij zijn afspraken zijn.' ... 'Alle maagjes savonds gevuld zijn...Dat het huis op zich toonbaar is.' ... 'Moe, uitgeput kom ik iedere dag uit het ziekenhuis.'
key_findings.geography: NL (31-year-old woman, married, one son, breast cancer dx Jan 2023)

key_findings.finding: A chemo day is effectively a full workday consumed: in two first-person accounts (UK and US), patients are collected at 7:15-7:20am and are not home until after 3pm, ~7-8 hours door-to-door, much of it bloodwork, cannula attempts, and waiting.
key_findings.evidence: UK: 'Start hydrating ... 7:15 ... Treatment starts. Infusion of Taxol lasts an hour ... I'm actually out of there around 3pm.' US: 'My day begins with my lovely friend picking me up at 7:20.'
key_findings.geography: UK (Fran Whitfield) and US (Alabama, Donna Brooks at medium.com/@donnaeichbrooks)

key_findings.finding: Treatment patients lean on others just to move: the chemo day depends on a friend driving both ways, and patients rotate multiple drivers to avoid burning out any one person.
key_findings.evidence: 'My amazing trusty friend picks me up from Kirklin and takes me home.' ... patients have 'multiple people taking turns to avoid caregiver burnout.'

key_findings.finding: In the NL, the return-to-work / sick-leave system is a slow, poorly-guided admin track: only 45% of survivors were actually guided by a bedrijfsarts/insurance physician, and those guided rated that guidance just 4.6/10.
key_findings.evidence: Only 45 percent were guided by an occupational or insurance physician ... patients feeling misunderstood and giving the occupational physician guidance a rating of 4.6.
key_findings.geography: NL (NFK 'Doneer je Ervaring' survey, ~3,500 survivors + 602 relatives)

key_findings.finding: NL re-integration is structurally delayed because the problem analysis and reintegration plan are typically postponed until after treatment ends, stretching the trajectory by roughly a year.
key_findings.evidence: The problem with cancer is that the treatment makes you sick, so the problem analysis and reintegration plan are often postponed until after treatments, meaning a year passes.

key_findings.finding: Money admin is a long-tail burden in the NL: 75-76% of (ex-)cancer patients report adverse financial consequences, half saw income drop within a year of diagnosis, and for half of 2,391 patients the situation had not recovered after five years.
key_findings.evidence: 76% van de mensen met of na kanker ervaart nadelige financiële gevolgen ... de helft ... zagen hun inkomen dalen, vaak binnen een jaar na diagnose. Bij de helft van 2391 patiënten was de financiële situatie na vijf jaar nog niet hersteld.

key_findings.finding: Even within the NL's covered system, recurring out-of-pocket admin grinds: the annual eigen risico is consumed by routine controls, and costs like parking, transport and partially-reimbursed aids are the patient's own — and only 3% got financial help via a care professional.
key_findings.evidence: 'Elk jaar moet ik nog op controle in het ziekenhuis. Daar gaat mijn eigen risico al aan op.' ... Parkeerkosten zijn altijd voor eigen rekening ... Slechts 3 procent kreeg hulp via de zorgprofessional.

key_findings.finding: The admin/logistics burden now has a clinical name — 'logistic toxicity' — distinct from financial toxicity, capturing care coordination, insurance navigation, and scheduling as a treatment side effect in their own right.
key_findings.evidence: The article explicitly introduces 'logistic toxicity' as a term describing the administrative and coordination burdens cancer survivors face—distinct from financial toxicity ... 'a real burden to individuals at a time when they would prefer to focus on living.'

key_findings.finding: Coordinating care is described by patients/caregivers as 'a crash course in juggling' multiple specialties, scans, bloodwork and biopsies, with ripple effects onto families, work and personal life.
key_findings.evidence: Caring for someone with cancer feels like a crash course in juggling ... keep track of appointments between multiple specialties, like radiation oncology or surgical oncology, and testing ... multiple scans, bloodwork, or biopsies.

key_findings.finding: Working patients feel the time burden most acutely, and a personal calendar starts to mirror a work calendar in density.
key_findings.evidence: 'My personal calendar started to look as busy as my work calendar.' ... Working participants were significantly more likely than retired ones to prioritize time reduction (58% vs. 36.5% for travel time).
key_findings.geography: Scotland/UK (LBBC blog) + US (PMC12128304 OOCAT study, n=224)

key_findings.finding: When fatigue hits, the practical fallout is that basics — showering, dressing, cooking, housework — become the things that get dropped, and patients are explicitly advised to outsource cooking/housework and lower standards.
key_findings.evidence: Everyday activities like showering, dressing and cooking can be a major challenge ... ask for help from others or home care with other activities (such as cooking and housework) ... windows don't necessarily need to be cleaned monthly.

surprises: The biggest single time-sink in the US data is not treatment or even travel — it is fighting one's own insurer: 12% of patients (or their family) lost a full business week or more on a SINGLE prior-authorization request, and 95% of those requests were approved anyway. That is pure deadweight admin a daily companion could attack directly.

The 2-to-1 ratio is stark and underused as a framing: patients spend ~2 hours traveling and waiting for every 1 hour of actual treatment. The 'medical' part of cancer is the minority of the time cost.

Childcare is a silent driver of MISSED treatment, not just stress: nearly half of parents with cancer rescheduled oncology appointments over childcare and 1 in 7 radiotherapy patients missed appointments for it. Logistics failures translate directly into worse clinical outcomes.

The informal support network is structurally fragile by the numbers: 80%+ of childcare comes from family/friends, but 90% of those helpers have their own jobs and half have their own kids. The 'care circle' Ditto bets on is real but already maxed out — a tool that reduces coordination load on the circle, not just adds tasks, is the wedge.

Even in the heavily-insured NL system, financial damage is durable: for half of patients it had not recovered after FIVE years. The admin burden is not an acute-phase problem that ends with treatment — it has a years-long tail (eigen risico every year, re-integration, income).

The NL re-integration system is almost a mirror-image of the US insurance problem: instead of too many forced authorizations, the failure mode is too little guidance — only 45% got a bedrijfsarts at all, rated 4.6/10, with the plan deliberately postponed ~a year until after treatment.

There is already a clinical/advocacy vocabulary for this — 'logistic toxicity' (NCCS) and 'time toxicity' — which means a product positioned as reducing logistic/time toxicity can plug into an existing, credible narrative rather than inventing a category.
gaps_or_caveats: The single best quantitative time-use study (median 400 min/week, the 2:1 travel:treatment ratio, 35% disruption) is US-only, n=60, and limited to metastatic breast and advanced ovarian cancer women (median age 59, 77% White). It maps well onto Ditto's severe/oncology beachhead but does NOT give an NL number for hours/week — I found no equivalent Dutch time-use study quantifying weekly admin hours.

The prior-authorization numbers (51%/27%/12% time loss, 85% prevalence) are intrinsically US: they reflect private/Medicare utilization management. The NL equivalent burden is structured completely differently (eigen risico, UWV/bedrijfsarts re-integration, regiotaxi/zittend ziekenvervoer reimbursement), so US insurance-admin figures should NOT be transplanted to the NL roadmap.

Most granular task-level breakdowns (e.g. 'minutes per week on scheduling vs bills vs transport') collapse into a single 'at-home tasks' bucket of 209 min/week. The earlier search snippet claimed a 'median 13 min/week on scheduling/bills/transport with top quartile 1hr+', but I could not confirm that exact split in the full paper text I retrieved — treat that specific sub-figure as low confidence.

Dutch first-person texture is solid on the family/household/exhaustion dimension (kanker.nl diary) and on finances (NFK), but I could not find an NL diary that walks through the weekly APPOINTMENT-CALENDAR-COORDINATION load across departments in verbatim detail — that texture came from US/UK sources. A targeted NL forum dig (kanker.nl communities, Olijf, Hematon) would strengthen this.

Several rich primary sources were paywalled or blocked (Medscape 402, the JCO abstract 403, Susannah Fox caregiver essay 403, Donna Brooks Medium partially). The chemo-day timelines and the JCO 'distress' quantification are therefore reconstructed from search snippets and adjacent open sources rather than full-text.

Meal/nausea-specific time-use is thin: searches surfaced recipe/advice content rather than lived 'I couldn't cook this week' verbatims with numbers. The cooking-when-nauseous load is well-attested qualitatively (borstkanker.nl) but I have no time figure for it.
The medication '20 pills a day' figure comes from an oncology clinic's patient-tips page, not a study — directionally useful for texture, but not a research-grade prevalence number.

key_findings.finding: Asking for help is one of the hardest parts of cancer: nearly half of UK patients struggle to ask friends, family or colleagues, and fear of pity is the top reason.
key_findings.evidence: 47% of cancer patients found it difficult asking for help from friends, family and colleagues; 43% of those feared being pitied; 30% cited pressure to stay strong. Survey of 500 UK adults with cancer (Censuswide for Cancer Research UK/Race for Life, April 2019).

key_findings.finding: The asking-for-help barrier is sharply gendered: women find it far harder to reach out than men, and take longer to even disclose the diagnosis to loved ones.
key_findings.evidence: 58% of female cancer patients found it hard to reach out vs 36% of male patients. Women took an average of 10 days to discuss their diagnosis with loved ones, men 6 days.

key_findings.finding: Patients frame not asking for help as a refusal to burden others, identity-rooted in being 'the helper' not the helped.
key_findings.evidence: Chris (31, lung cancer): "I didn't want them to carry my burden." Esther (56, breast cancer): "I felt I needed to stay strong for my family." Meta-synthesis verbatim: "I have been the one who liked to support people, so I have never managed to be the one who needs help...Very difficult."

key_findings.finding: 'Cancer ghosting' is widespread: a majority of patients report friends or family withdrawing after diagnosis, and the abandonment lands as a second wound on top of the illness.
key_findings.evidence: One survey found 65% of respondents experienced cancer ghosting; more than 75% said friends or family withdrew since diagnosis. Georgie Swallow (27, UK): "For that to stop, and your friends to stop even coming to see you, it's just another hit that you take when you're already going through so much."

key_findings.finding: Friends withdraw because the patient reminds them of death, not from lack of care, and the silence is never explained.
key_findings.evidence: Yamour Yapici (25, UK): "Some of my friends just didn't know how to handle it. They felt quite afraid, so they avoided seeing me because I reminded them of death." "They didn't want to be emotionally traumatised by the whole process of watching me deteriorate."

key_findings.finding: Loneliness coexists with attention: patients feel alone in a full house and believe no one without the lived experience can understand.
key_findings.evidence: Meta-synthesis verbatim (USA): "There could be everybody home in my house and I still feel really alone." Another: "I want to see no one because I feel nobody can understand."

key_findings.finding: Most patients default to silence about their cancer to avoid misunderstanding or to protect others, and many never initiate the conversation at all.
key_findings.evidence: Meta-synthesis: 80% of patients choose silence, primarily fearing misunderstanding or to protect others; 35% never initiate discussion about the illness and 24% only discuss it when prompted.

key_findings.finding: Repeatedly updating everyone is a recurring weekly drain; patients describe being 'sick and tired' of retelling the story and resort to a single point-person or group post to survive it.
key_findings.evidence: "I got sick and tired of repeating the same story every time someone asked." Patients found "telling the basic story once via social media and group email was easier, emotionally, than the difficult and exhausting process of many, many phone calls."

key_findings.finding: Patients tire of being defined by cancer in every interaction and feel the relationship has become one-directional.
key_findings.evidence: Ellen: "I'm so tired of the discussion being about me all the time." Michele: "Even with support, I feel alone because I just CAN'T talk about it." Tara: "When active treatment is complete, it's over for them. It's never really over for us."

key_findings.finding: The visit economy carries a hosting cost: managing friendships while sick is itself exhausting labour, separate from the illness.
key_findings.evidence: Shine Cancer Support blog (UK): "managing your friendships can be exhausting when you're also managing your health, and worrying about the future." ACS guidance notes patients can emotionally handle only "one or two reveals" of the diagnosis a day before it feels "exhausting and very blue."

key_findings.finding: Being the focus of concern can itself feel othering, turning the patient into a spectacle rather than a person.
key_findings.evidence: Meta-synthesis verbatim: "It got to the point where I was beginning to find it rather strange to be the focus of so much attention, I felt like a freak." And from Iran: "I hurt to meet people's pitying look...I hate to hear this word."

key_findings.finding: Intimacy and sex collapse during treatment, and partner withdrawal is experienced as humiliation and a loss of gender identity.
key_findings.evidence: Meta-synthesis verbatims: "After having a mastectomy, my ex-husband didn't sleep with me and didn't touch me at all. I was humiliated." "He just pulled away...I was furious [You] cannot just disappear when things get difficult!" "Prostatectomy affected my sexual relationship...She told me I was no longer a man."

key_findings.finding: Sexuality becomes an active, painful effort rather than a given; desire vanishes and intercourse hurts, requiring patients to 'fight for' it.
key_findings.evidence: Cervical cancer survivor (divorced, 46, Israel): "You need to fight for your sexuality...You don't feel like it, it hurts, it does not bring you pleasure, all of your sexuality is gone." Another (married, 41): "I have no desire for it...they took away my joy in life."

key_findings.finding: Partners are often present for logistics but emotionally absent, creating a specific loneliness inside the couple.
key_findings.evidence: Cervical cancer survivor (married, 45, Israel): "My husband will do everything that is necessary...But that's it...for anything related to emotions, to closeness, he's simply not there."

key_findings.finding: Sexual dysfunction is near-universal for young women in treatment, the physical substrate behind the relational strain.
key_findings.evidence: Sexual dysfunction in at least one domain was reported by 68% of young women with breast cancer; high reproductive concerns in at least one dimension by 58%.

key_findings.finding: The daily school run is where a mother's cancer becomes socially visible and isolating, set against other parents' apparent normalcy.
key_findings.evidence: Ann Coxon (London): "As other mothers breezily arrived at the Reception classroom door, pushing buggies with months-old younger siblings in tow, it also dawned on me that I may well be the only menopausal mother at the school gate." Describes "juggling school book bags, water bottles, school trip forms, my own work bag" on the 15-minute walk to school.

key_findings.finding: Chemo weeks remove the mother from family life for days at a time, and accepting help to fill the gap triggers guilt.
key_findings.evidence: Stella (UK): "I was completely zapped by chemotherapy. I couldn't be present for my family like I usually was. I was in bed more often than not" and "out of it for close to a week" per cycle. Marije: "When my husband's parents stepped in to help, I felt guilty about it."

key_findings.finding: Parents script the diagnosis for kids around routine and reassurance, using calendars to show who does drop-off/pickup and metaphors children grasp.
key_findings.evidence: Lilly Ribner: "I explained that my port was the fairy door through which minions (their favorite movie at the time) traveled to deliver the medicine"; daughter responded "Bye bye, cancer! I don't like you, cancer!" Guidance: "use a calendar to show your kids what to expect each day - from who is doing school drop-off and pick-up to what treatments you're having."

key_findings.finding: Returning to work means navigating awkward colleague dynamics, fear of being smothered with sympathy, and a lasting stigma of unreliability.
key_findings.evidence: Cited survivor: "I told only a few colleagues about my diagnosis. I couldn't handle being smothered in sympathy every time I walked down the hall." zeppogirl: "I feel like I do have the stigma of being unreliable, like, 'Hmm, maybe she'll get sick again and can we trust her with more responsibility.'"

key_findings.finding: Friendships are binary under cancer: some intensify, many simply go silent, with no explanation given.
key_findings.evidence: Meta-synthesis (USA): "all my other friends, I never hear from them. I call them, they don't call me back." "You know through this sickness, almost all my people changed." Refinery29 (UK), Lydia Brain on a close friend: "I never felt like she was there for me...she was just gone."

key_findings.finding: The patient's cancer reshapes the wider family's relationships too, including adult children who feel shut out and lack their own support.
key_findings.evidence: Sally (London): "people who receive the news together often form a tightly bonded club. I know this is true of my parents, and I felt left on the outside"; "I was desperate for his emotional support, but unsure of how to ask for it"; "I didn't feel that there was enough support for me. The focus at the clinic...was on my mum."

surprises: The asking-for-help barrier is driven specifically by fear of PITY (43%), not fear of rejection or logistics - patients would rather go without than be looked at with sympathy. This reframes the product opportunity: low-friction, dignity-preserving help-coordination matters more than the help itself.

Loneliness is strongest INSIDE the home and inside the couple, not from absence of people. 'There could be everybody home in my house and I still feel really alone' and partners who 'do everything necessary' but are emotionally 'simply not there.' Attention does not equal connection.

Updating everyone is a distinct, recurring weekly labour that patients actively dread and engineer around (one point-person, group posts). This is a concrete, repeatable JTBD that fires every treatment cycle, not a one-time event.

The visit economy has a real hosting cost the patient pays: managing friendships and 'reveals' is exhausting work layered on top of being sick, and being the focus of concern can make patients feel like 'a freak.' Support can be experienced as a tax.

Several patients describe relationships ending in silence with NO explanation ever given - the ambiguity itself is part of the wound, suggesting value in tools that reduce the social awkwardness others feel around reaching out.

Cancer's relational damage extends a ring outward: adult children of patients report feeling shut out of the 'club' and having no support of their own because clinical focus is on the patient and primary caregiver - a care-circle gap Ditto's model could address.
gaps_or_caveats: The brief's '45-60% need support more often than they ask' framing maps best to the Cancer Research UK 2019 survey (47% find it hard to ask; 58% of women), but I did not find a source using that exact 45-60% range or that exact phrasing - treat it as a paraphrase of adjacent UK survey figures.

Most strong first-person verbatims are UK and US; explicit NL/Dutch primary voices are thin. One quoted mother ('Marije') and the meta-synthesis (which lists the Netherlands among nine source countries) are the closest Dutch-context signals. Oncology-specific Dutch patient diaries were not surfaced.

The 65%/75% cancer-ghosting figures come via a secondary report (Refinery29 citing a survey); I could not open the primary CURE/breastcancer.org survey writeups (HTTP 403) to confirm sample size and methodology, so confidence on those exact numbers is medium.

Several high-value sources blocked WebFetch (403): CURE, Today.com, Young Survival Coalition, Mayo Clinic Connect, Cancer Today, CSN forum. Forum-level raw verbatims (Reddit, CSN, Mayo Connect threads) are under-sampled because search/fetch could not reach them; the texture leans on curated blogs and qualitative studies rather than unfiltered forum chatter.

Quantified 'cost per week' of maintaining relationships is largely absent in patients' own words - they describe it qualitatively (exhausting, a full-time job, days lost per chemo cycle) rather than in hours or money. The closest concrete unit is 'close to a week' of being non-functional per chemo cycle (Stella, UK) and the 'one or two reveals per day' ceiling.

The intimacy/sex verbatims skew female (breast, cervical) and toward heterosexual partnerships; male-patient and same-sex partner relational texture is thin, with prostate cancer represented by a single quote.

key_findings.finding: Chemo brain isn't just slow word-recall; people lose the thread of their own sentence while speaking and can't name an object they're looking at.
key_findings.evidence: "With chemo brain, I can forget what I'm even talking about while I'm talking about it. I can't find common words, like tree, as I'm looking at one!"

key_findings.finding: Reading collapses within a single paragraph: comprehension is lost between the first sentence and the last, and simple recipes become unfollowable.
key_findings.evidence: "by the time I got to the last sentence in a paragraph, I could not remember what I had read in the first sentence." and "after chemo, I couldn't even follow a simple recipe."

key_findings.finding: Chemo brain fires as concrete daily errors: forgetting items repeatedly mid-errand, losing the parked car, leaving rooms empty-handed. These are discrete failure events, not a vague fog.
key_findings.evidence: "The grocery store...took two and a half hours because I forgot my wallet, my bag, my keys, then finally the list." (Carol); "I couldn't remember where I put my car. It took me over an hour." (M.E. Henitz); "I go upstairs to get the laundry and I'll come down without it." (Cathy)
key_findings.geography: US (qualitative study, women with early-stage breast cancer)

key_findings.finding: The dominant chemo-brain workaround is external memory offloading: pocket lists added to throughout the day, and a fixed daily alarm specifically to trigger medication.
key_findings.evidence: "I make lists and carry them in my pocket so I can add to them." (Julie); "I set my alarm every day at the same time." (Cathy, for medication)

key_findings.finding: Word-finding failure interrupts ordinary conversation at the dinner table, with the person stalling on a single everyday word ('salt') they need repeatedly.
key_findings.evidence: "I'd be sat at the dinner table, saying, 'Can you pass me the…um…um…?' and the word wouldn't come out." / "I would just stop mid-conversation because I couldn't think of the right word."

key_findings.finding: Taste loss is progressive and ends in a metallic baseline where food vanishes entirely as a flavor, not just tastes 'off'.
key_findings.evidence: "Then the taste of food disappeared altogether, and everything started tasting like metal." (Glen Haubold)

key_findings.finding: Specific foods flip from safe to repulsive in ways that are idiosyncratic and texture/acid-driven: bread turns bitter, tomato becomes ammonia or paste, red meat and coffee become inedible.
key_findings.evidence: "Bread for example was really bitter"; "Spaghetti tasted like tomato paste, watermelon like ammonia." (Bette); "Coffee was foul"; "Went off red meats"

key_findings.finding: What people actually manage to eat clusters around cold, sweet, acidic, and frozen items: ice lollies, sorbet, vanilla ice cream, cold melon/grapes, tinned fruit, yoghurt, custard, cola. Cold and sweet survive when hot and savory don't.
key_findings.evidence: "Lemonade ice lollies, lemon sorbet and vanilla ice cream"; "melon chunks (if you can get them really cold)"; "Yoghurts, smoothies, milkshakes, cereal, custard, rice pudding"; "Sweet things taste vaguely normal so I try to eat by alternating a mouthful of food with a slug of Ribena." (SamKatz)

key_findings.finding: Cooking smells, not just taste, are a primary daily barrier to eating; hot/savory food smells trigger nausea so people retreat to cold sandwiches, tinned fruit, and sweet drinks.
key_findings.evidence: "I have no appetite to speak of and can't stand the smell of food cooking." / "It's mainly hot / savoury food I can't stand. But even sandwiches turn my stomach." (ColinD)

key_findings.finding: Eating becomes a clock-driven defensive routine: some patients learn they must eat on a fixed interval to prevent symptom collapse, turning food into scheduled maintenance rather than meals.
key_findings.evidence: "We learned that I have to eat every two hours or the shit hits the fan."
key_findings.geography: US (chemo diary blog, breast cancer, mother of young kids)

key_findings.finding: Steroids drive a manic-then-crash micro-cycle: nights of 3-4 hours sleep followed by frantic daytime activity (deep-cleaning the house), then an emotional collapse despite feeling physically fine.
key_findings.evidence: "I only got 3 and 1/2 hours sleep last night... I went crazy with the housework in the afternoon... the steroids must be working overtime" and "physically I am feeling fine, mentally I am broken into pieces"

key_findings.finding: Sleep architecture is destroyed in fragments, not just shortened: floaty pre-sleep states, two-hour sleep blocks, and hypnic jerks that yank the body awake at the threshold of sleep.
key_findings.evidence: "Felt slightly out of body, floaty...went to bed at around 6pm...slept for perhaps two hours at a time" (Macmillan diary, Day 1); "Every time that you're about to fall asleep, it feels like someone is startling you awake–except it's your own body... my legs would jerk or my arms would twitch."

key_findings.finding: Energy is budgeted in discrete, countable units (the 'spoon' frame is widely adopted), and in heavy treatment a whole day's allowance may be one or two acts: getting out of bed, or a shower.
key_findings.evidence: "Wake up and fix breakfast, one spoon; take a shower, one spoon; get dressed, one spoon..." and "maybe I had two spoons—one for getting out of bed and moving to the sofa, and a second spoon for going to bed at night."

key_findings.finding: The 'shower-as-achievement' phenomenon is real and quantified by patients as one-of-three: they can do a single discretionary activity per day and must choose between hygiene, errands, or social contact.
key_findings.evidence: "I typically had enough energy to do one thing each day—take a shower, or go to Target, or go to lunch with a friend—but I couldn't do all three."

key_findings.finding: Neuropathy registers as a constant phantom-sock barrier between the body and the world: the floor can't be felt, causing trips and stumbles on flat carpet.
key_findings.evidence: "It felt like she was wearing socks all the time, even when she was barefoot. 'I couldn't always tell when my foot was touching the ground,' she says. 'I was tripping over the carpet at times.'" (patient Oehler)

key_findings.finding: Neuropathy makes fingers feel painfully frozen though they're warm to the touch, and patients ration phone use and improvise hand tools to cope with the constant sensation.
key_findings.evidence: "my fingers are numb and feel painfully freezing to me, although not cold to touch"; workarounds: "limit phone use", "finger massage ring", "squeezing a rubber toy ball", washing-up gloves for tepid water

key_findings.finding: Cold becomes weaponized by neuropathy (especially oxaliplatin/taxanes): touching cold objects is crippling, forcing patients to wear mittens for routine tasks like opening the fridge.
key_findings.evidence: "Cold sensations would cripple me (so I had mittens for everything)." (Theresa); "I really struggled with smells while on Taxanes and also when on Platins."

key_findings.finding: Self-managed oral care is a multiple-times-daily ritual to keep mouth sores survivable; baking-soda rinses recur as the most-cited DIY protocol.
key_findings.evidence: "I rinsed my mouth out with a mixture of baking soda and water multiple times a day." (Connie Porter, Ph.D.)

key_findings.finding: A single day-by-day diary shows how fast symptoms rotate: taste gone by Day 2 (couldn't taste bacon), heartburn-driven food elimination by Day 6-9, mouth feeling 'strange' Day 4, hair loss Day 8 - the daily companion target changes within one cycle.
key_findings.evidence: Day 2: "Bacon, couldn't taste it!"; Day 6: "Had strawberry yoghurt closely followed by Diet Coke and got heartburn"; Day 9: "First day with no heartburn as a result of avoiding all fruit"; Day 4: "Mouth still strange."

key_findings.finding: Dutch (NL) patient voices mirror the same micro-reality: night-waking to eat, appetite arriving 'in waves', taste changing daily, and trivial acts (picking up coat and shoes) feeling exhausting.
key_findings.evidence: "vannacht ben ik opgestaan om mijn maag te vullen met een bakje skyr, ik kon niet slapen" (got up at night to fill my stomach with skyr, couldn't sleep); "De trek komt in golven" (appetite comes in waves); "alleen al het pakken van mijn jas en schoenen voelde zo uitputtend" (just getting my coat and shoes felt so exhausting); "elke dag was mijn smaak anders"

key_findings.finding: Time-keeping itself breaks down as a chemo-brain symptom, independent of memory: patients become chronically, structurally late and miss scheduled calls.
key_findings.evidence: "I cannot make it anywhere on time." (Carol); "We started about 10 minutes ago and we didn't want to call and bother you." (Sherry, on missing a work call)

key_findings.finding: Mornings are reported as the worst window of the day, with patients winded within minutes of waking while trying to maintain a child's routine.
key_findings.evidence: "Mornings seem to be the hardest. I wake up and try to tend to the kids for their own sense of normalcy and my own, but then I am quickly winded."

surprises: The 'shower-as-achievement' phenomenon is concretely quantified by patients themselves as a one-of-three daily tradeoff (shower OR errand OR a friend), not just generic tiredness. A daily companion that helped people pre-spend their single 'spoon' wisely would map directly onto how patients already think.

Eating becomes clock-driven defense, not appetite: at least one patient learned she must eat every two hours 'or the shit hits the fan.' This reframes the food battle as a timed-reminder problem (when to eat) as much as a what-can-I-eat problem.

Steroids create a predictable manic-up / crash-down micro-cycle within each chemo cycle (sleepless wired night, frantic 4pm cleaning, then emotional collapse the next day). This is rhythmic and forecastable per-cycle, which is exactly the kind of pattern a daily AI companion could anticipate rather than react to.

Taste isn't a single stable deficit; it changes day to day ('elke dag was mijn smaak anders' / 'every day my taste was different'), so any food guidance must be re-asked daily, not stored once. The 'safe food' list has a 24-hour shelf life.

Chemo brain manifests as discrete, nameable failure EVENTS (forgot wallet then bag then keys then list at one shop; lost the car for an hour; came downstairs without the laundry) rather than a constant haze. These are the moments an in-the-moment assistant could intercept.

Neuropathy degrades the exact input channel an app relies on: numb/painfully-cold fingers make people 'limit phone use' and struggle to type. A daily companion for this population may need large touch targets, voice-first input, and cold-tolerant interaction, or it fails precisely when needed most.

Cold and sweet foods survive when nothing else does (ice lollies, sorbet, vanilla ice cream, cold melon/grapes), and acid (lemon, Ribena/blackcurrant) is used as a taste-reset trick. There is a recurring, near-universal 'safe palette' that could be packaged as concrete daily suggestions.
gaps_or_caveats: Most rich verbatims are US and UK; only one strong NL/EU primary source (Kanker.nl) was captured. Dutch-language patient diaries and forums (kanker.nl, borstkanker.nl) likely hold far more EU-specific texture and should be mined directly, ideally via the user-researcher/NotebookLM path or native Dutch search, since US-only web search under-surfaces them.

Several high-yield first-person sources (Sharsheret mucositis essay, Cancer Health 'Dozen Chemo Thoughts', Lungevity and Cancer Survivors Network steroid threads, Cancer Today neuropathy) returned 403/redirect and could not be quoted; verbatims for steroid-night detail and mouth-sore meal-by-meal accounts are thinner than the other categories as a result.

Medication-mistake specifics (took the wrong pill, double dose) were inferred from clinical sources and the 'forgot which pill' framing but I could not capture a clean first-person 'I took the wrong dose' verbatim; this exact failure mode needs a dedicated forum dig to confirm with a real quote.

Cancer type skews to breast cancer and a few GI/blood/pancreatic voices; oncology beachhead specifics (e.g., the daily reality on weekly oncology regimens, or head/neck where mouth sores dominate) are under-represented and worth a targeted pass.

Forum verbatims are self-selected and skew toward people well enough to post; the sickest days (bedridden, 'two spoons total') are described in retrospect, so the absolute worst-day texture is likely undercounted relative to its frequency.
Quotes were extracted via a summarizing fetch model; before any are used externally, re-verify each verbatim against the source page for exact wording and attribution.

key_findings.finding: The night before every scan result reactivates acute fear on a fixed cycle, and patients explicitly say it never gets routine even after being declared cured.
key_findings.evidence: "Die laatste dag, die laatste avond voor een uitslag komt de spanning terug, maar ook de angst." and "De komende twee jaar zal ik nog elke drie maanden in spanning zitten. Dat is wat kanker is." and "Wachten op een uitslag. Ik denk dat het nooit zal wennen."

key_findings.finding: Treatment is experienced as a relentless cycle where recovery never completes before the next cure starts, collapsing any sense of a normal week.
key_findings.evidence: "Ziekenhuisbezoek na ziekenhuisbezoek, chemo na chemo. Er lijkt geen einde." and "Als je net opgeknapt bent, begint volgende kuur alweer." (Jade Kops, breast cancer)

key_findings.finding: The body itself becomes the daily clock: ordinary actions like climbing the stairs or sitting on the couch register fatigue, and patients track their decline through these micro-failures.
key_findings.evidence: "De trap oplopen werd uiteindelijk ook een uitdaging. Ik was kapot als ik boven was." and "Ik was zelfs moe als ik op de bank zat. Zo raar." and "Dat soort kleine dingen, daarin merk je dat je achteruit gaat." (Annemijn van Leek, 25, breast cancer)

key_findings.finding: Taste collapse turns daily rituals into aversions: coffee, a normal morning pleasure, becomes repulsive in the days after a cure.
key_findings.evidence: "Vóór de kuur genoot ik nog van mijn kop koffie, de dagen daarna moest ik niet meer aan koffie denken." and "Je smaak is ineens heel erg vies. Dat vond ik zo irritant."

key_findings.finding: The hardest part is not treatment but life AFTER it ends: the 'zwarte gat' where the patient feels physically worse and less recovered emotionally than during treatment, while everyone assumes they are done.
key_findings.evidence: "Ik dacht: ik wandel het ziekenhuis uit na mijn laatste behandeling en ben weer gezond. Maar eigenlijk voelde het fysiek precies tegenovergesteld." and "Na het ziekenhuis begint het pas, hoor ik van veel ex-patiënten." and "Ik bleek veel minder ver te zijn in mijn verwerking dan ik dacht." (Marleen)

key_findings.finding: Cognitive damage (chemobrein) and sensory overstimulation are felt DAILY for many months and force a hidden re-engineering of life that is invisible to outsiders.
key_findings.evidence: "Gevolgen van de behandelingen voel ik nog dagelijks." and "Je bent heel snel overprikkeld en hebt een slechte concentratie." and "Voor de buitenwereld ziet het eruit alsof ik gewoon doorga, maar eigenlijk heb ik m'n hele leven erop aangepast." and "Ik ben een veranderd mens in hetzelfde leven." (Linda Hakeboom; reported 18 months of severe chemobrein)

key_findings.finding: A specific recurring social friction is the phrase 'wat zie je er nog goed uit' — well-meant but cutting, because it implies cancer must mean visibly bedridden and pale, and forces the patient to manage others' mental image.
key_findings.evidence: "Wat zie je er nog goed uit ??? verbazing alom. Hoe kan dat nou, jij hebt toch kanker ???" and "waarom dan het woordje 'nog'?" and "Als je maar al te goed weet dat ze dat mechanisch zeggen, omdat het een standaardzin is, dan is het eerder kwetsend dan helpend."

key_findings.finding: Patients would rather people say clumsy or stupid things than avoid them; social avoidance (people crossing the street, hiding in the supermarket) is experienced as worse than awkward questions.
key_findings.evidence: "Ik heb liever dat mijn omgeving ''domme'' dingen tegen me zegt, dan dat ze me negeren en zelfs niet meer ''durven'' komen." and "Hij stak zijn hand op met de woorden: hé leef jij nog?"

key_findings.finding: The casual Dutch greeting 'hoe gaat het?' is itself a daily burden: there is no good answer, the patient does not want to tell everyone the truth, yet the honest answer is just 'slecht'.
key_findings.evidence: "En op de vraag hoe gaat het ermee kan je eigenlijk maar 1 ting zeggen: Slecht." and "Je wil ook niet iederéén vertellen hoe het werkelijk met je gaat." and "Liefst zou ik hebben dat ze niet vragen hoe gaat het, maar actief helpen." (partner/caregiver)

key_findings.finding: The caregiver day has its own breaking point separate from the patient: the partner reaches moments of being unable to even listen, and wants practical help over questions.
key_findings.evidence: "Ik ben er zó klaar mee. Ik kan en wíl hem even niet horen." and "Ik hoef deze vraag nu even niet ik kan er niets mee." and "Liefst zou ik hebben dat ze niet vragen hoe gaat het, maar actief helpen."

key_findings.finding: The diagnosis splits time into a hard before/after with a literal start date the patient counts toward, and the infusion schedule becomes the only certainty in life.
key_findings.evidence: "Het is zaterdag, en alles is anders... Maandag begint er een nieuw, onzeker leven voor mij. Vanaf maandag lig ik 54 weken aan het infuus. Dat is het enige zekere dat ik nog heb." (Sophie van der Stap, Meisje met negen pruiken)

key_findings.finding: On a chemo day the burden is split between managing one's own fear and managing the family's day, especially shielding a child going to school for a test.
key_findings.evidence: "Angst verdriet alles doet mee deze ochtend." and "Hup zoon lief naar school. Balen voor dat ventje een toets en een moeder die vandaag naar de Oncologie moet." and "Al die tijd kan ik beter aan mijn zoon besteden. Huiswerk, ijsje eten iets. Niet voor mijn haar."

key_findings.finding: For younger patients the dominant daily emotion is social exile and loss of role: not looking sick, yet having no future perspective and being cut out of working society.
key_findings.evidence: "Het is het soms gewoon ontzettend eenzaam, je maakt geen deel meer uit van de maatschappij." and "Ik zie er namelijk niet ziek uit, maar heb ook geen toekomstperspectief." and "Mijn werk mis ik echt enorm." (Sorsha, 30)

key_findings.finding: Distinctly Dutch: home care (thuiszorg) and the portable chemo pump mean treatment physically continues inside the home and handbag, blurring hospital and daily life.
key_findings.evidence: "Met mijn chemopomp in mijn handtas, moet ik proberen te accepteren." and "Na thuiszorg afgelopen dinsdag... chemopomp aangesloten." (Jade Kops)

key_findings.finding: The practical/admin load is a documented week-to-week machine: insurance coverage checks, regiotaxi/zittend ziekenvervoer reimbursement, packing hospital bags, rosters of helpers, online groceries, notifying employer/school — a parallel job alongside being ill.
key_findings.evidence: Kanker.nl checklist lists verbatim tasks incl. "Vergoeding voor een regiotaxi of zittend ziekenvervoer", "Ga met je partner of naaste mee naar het ziekenhuis", rosters for household help, online grocery delivery, and notifying school/employer.

key_findings.finding: For advanced/metastatic patients the daily texture is explicit oscillation between good and bad moments, with self-soothing rituals scheduled around medical procedures.
key_findings.evidence: "De goede momenten maar ook de slechte momenten." and "even mijn hart luchten vandaag had ik de lumbaal punctie" and "Hier zit ik dan nu in een heerlijk geurend bad, kaarsjes aan muziekje aan te stressen!" (Embraced by Nathalie / Dagboek van een onbekende)

key_findings.finding: The world physically shrinks day by day for chronically/terminally ill patients, who track being incrementally more tired each day and feel moedeloos at small undone tasks like the garden.
key_findings.evidence: "mijn wereld steeds een beetje kleiner wordt, dat ik elke dag een stukje moeier word" and "de tuin roept…. Kom, je wordt blij van ons…Moedeloos word ik ervan… ik wil zo graag" and "ik vind de jaarlijkse controle zo verschrikkelijk confronterend"

key_findings.finding: Repetitive medical identity-verification rituals become a grinding daily marker of patienthood, said with weariness.
key_findings.evidence: "Voor de tienduizendste keer noem ik mijn geboortedatum." and "Ik sta er mee op en ik ga er mee naar bed... Geen minuut voorbij." (Jade Kops)

key_findings.finding: Embodied grief for the pre-cancer body is a recurring daily emotion, distinct from fear of death.
key_findings.evidence: "Ik mis mijn oude lichaam... hier kan ik niet zoveel moois van maken." and "Kilo na kilo, traan na traan. Het was niet meer te doen." (Jade Kops)

key_findings.finding: Distinctly Dutch: the huisarts (GP) is woven into the cancer and end-of-life journey as a continuous figure, surfaced in mainstream NPO/KRO-NCRV documentary culture about living and dying with cancer.
key_findings.evidence: KRO-NCRV documentary 'Dying to Live' follows Mirjam Willemsen, a huisarts who guides terminally ill patients while herself being incurably ill with lung cancer, including the moment a CT scan shows the cancer returned.

surprises: The single most repeated daily/weekly friction point in Dutch primary voices is not a medical symptom but a social-linguistic one: the casual greeting 'hoe gaat het?' and the compliment 'wat zie je er nog goed uit' are described as actively painful because they force the patient to manage other people's mental image of cancer. This is a distinctly Dutch surface (the directness and the obligatory polite question) and is a clear product opening for a companion that helps patients script or deflect these encounters.

Patients overwhelmingly report that the WORST period is AFTER treatment ends (the 'zwarte gat'), not during it — the opposite of the public assumption. The app's center of gravity arguably should extend past the last chemo, exactly when hospital touchpoints (and current summary products) drop to zero.

Multiple patients say they would rather people say clumsy/stupid things than avoid them entirely; social avoidance (people crossing the street, hiding behind toilet rolls in the supermarket) is experienced as worse than any awkward question. The care circle's failure mode is silence, not saying the wrong thing.

The chemo pump in the handbag (chemopomp in mijn handtas) via thuiszorg means treatment is literally carried through daily life in NL — a concrete, distinctly Dutch home-care detail that dissolves the hospital/home boundary the summary product assumes.

Caregivers hit their own daily breaking point ('Ik ben er zó klaar mee. Ik kan en wíl hem even niet horen') and explicitly prefer practical help over emotional check-ins — pointing to a care-circle coordination job (rosters, groceries, transport) rather than another emotional-support surface.
