gaps_or_caveats: WebFetch returned quotes via a summarizer model; while instructed to quote verbatim, exact punctuation/spelling of some Dutch quotes (especially typo-laden raw blog text) should be re-verified against the source before any are used in product copy or quoted publicly.

The Sophie van der Stap and Maarten van der Weijden book quotes come from publisher/retailer pages and secondary summaries, not the primary book text; the Van der Weijden 'elke dag' angle could not be sourced to a direct passage (only the 'geluk/pech' framing was confirmed).

Instagram NL cancer accounts (e.g. @mijnlevenmetkanker_ ~448K followers per search, @lindahakeboom, @MaudvanOossanen, @steephy.breastcancer, @kimgringhuis, @noshameinmyscargame) were identified but not directly scraped — individual daily-life captions/verbatims from these feeds were not captured and would be a high-value next pass.

Most strong verbatims skew toward breast cancer and younger female patients (the dominant NL blogging/columnist demographic). Oncology beachhead voices for other tumor types, older patients, and male patients are underrepresented in this pass.

Stichting OOK and inloophuizen descriptions of 'what people come in with' were not obtained as verbatim first-person texture; searches surfaced only generic descriptions and Belgian inloophuis pages. A targeted pass on NL inloophuis intake themes is still open.
Geography flag: all primary daily-life voices captured here are NL (some Belgian/Flemish support pages appeared in results but were excluded). No US contamination in the cited findings.

key_findings.finding: In the diagnosis-to-treatment limbo, the waiting itself, not the treatment, is named as the worst part of the whole process, and a fast hospital callback is read as bad news.
key_findings.evidence: "Time runs slow when you are waiting" (Participant 4); "I received my call from the hospital already on the following Monday. It scared me because this had to be serious" (Participant 4)

key_findings.finding: During limbo, proactive communication about delays (even bad news like 'results aren't in yet') actively reduces distress, while unexplained gaps between urgent action and waiting are disturbing.
key_findings.evidence: "They called me and told me that 'I am sorry that we haven't received your results...it might be a few days more to wait'. This was good to know" (Participant 3); "a change of pace between urgent action and prolonged periods of waiting were disturbing"

key_findings.finding: In the limbo phase a single ambiguous word from a clinician becomes the object of obsessive rumination and catastrophic imagery; the dominant activity is fighting one's own intrusive thoughts.
key_findings.evidence: "Dat ene woordje, 'daar doelde hij vast op een slechte uitslag, op kanker'" (That single word, he must have meant a bad result, cancer); "De doembeelden nemen plaats in je hoofd en daarmee komt ook het verdriet" (Catastrophic images take hold in your mind, bringing grief with them)

key_findings.finding: Active treatment runs on a predictable intra-cycle rhythm: a 'couch day' / crash 2-4 days after infusion, then gradual recovery, so the week is structured around a known dip rather than diffuse illness.
key_findings.evidence: "The second day, I felt tired. The third day, I felt completely sick and immobilized. That lasted for 3 or 4 days. Then, gradually, I got better." (Heather Millar); a forum patient: "chemo on a Wednesday, red face day Thursday, then general feeling sick till Sunday"

key_findings.finding: Side effects are cumulative across cycles, so the same activity gets measurably harder cycle over cycle, and the worst crash can come after treatment ends, not during it.
key_findings.evidence: "For the first three cycles, I could make it to the top. But by the last cycle, it took me an hour just to get one-third of the way... The month after chemo was the hardest of all. I felt like I'd been run over by a truck." (Heather Millar)

key_findings.finding: The off-week between cycles follows a three-beat pattern on a 21-day cycle (rough week, slightly-better week, near-normal week), and the brief return to 'human' is immediately shadowed by the countdown to the next infusion.
key_findings.evidence: "one week feeling rough and totally exhausted, followed by one week of feeling a little better, then finally a week when I actually feel up to leaving the house... before tackling the next session"; "just before he starts a new round he feels almost like himself again in a 21-day cycle"

key_findings.finding: The end of treatment triggers an emotional fallout: the structure and reassurance of three-weekly hospital contact vanishes, leaving patients feeling left to fate exactly when they finally process what happened to them.
key_findings.evidence: "you go to the hospital every three weeks, you come out of that chemo miserable, someone says: it's going well, hang on. And then that's done, then you no longer..." (Man, 46, 3 months post-treatment); "when the check-ups are done you are just left to fate" (Woman, 52, 4 years post-treatment)

key_findings.finding: In the first year post-treatment, the support network's help evaporates the moment treatment ends; offers of help do not convert to actual help, and friends/family revert to pre-cancer behaviour while celebrating that it's 'over'.
key_findings.evidence: "The people around me, my friends, said: 'If you need help, we will be there for you!' But actually, if I would need something, no one comes to help me." (Woman, 48, 9 months post-treatment); from NZ study: "they get to the end of treatment, and family and friends are celebrating...relationships often go back to how they were pre-cancer"

key_findings.finding: Re-entry survivors carry a 'gratitude burden': they feel they should be grateful to be alive and are reluctant to voice distress, which suppresses help-seeking in the exact window when support has dropped off.
key_findings.evidence: "'I'm living, and I should be grateful, but I just want to cry. I'm anxious, I'm overwhelmed and really emotional. What's wrong with me?'"; "They are often reluctant to seek help because they feel ungrateful for bringing those kinds of things up."

key_findings.finding: Survivors explicitly miss the on-demand safety net of active treatment; the loss of an easy channel to ask 'is this normal / should I worry' is itself a distinct unmet need.
key_findings.evidence: "I know when I was in treatment, I could ring the ward... Whereas now... what do I do if I'm worried about something?"

key_findings.finding: For metastatic/chronic patients the dominant unit of time is scan-to-scan: the brief post-scan 'free' window of relative calm, then escalating dread building for days/weeks toward the next scan, repeating indefinitely.
key_findings.evidence: "My next control is in March, but before that it's just like I'm free, you know, a period in which I can somehow relax, before I begin to dread the next CT." (metastatic GIST patient); "held their breath 'for 72 hours every 3 months'"
key_findings.geography: EU (Norway) + scanxiety study (56% North America, 33% UK)

key_findings.finding: Scanxiety persists for years and does not habituate with repetition; the gap between scan and result is the acute peak, and it costs whole weeks of functional life.
key_findings.evidence: "86 times and I still get scanxiety"; "the last month has been lost to scanxiety"; Dutch metastatic patient: "De vijf werkdagen tussen scan en uitslag zijn veel zwaarder" (The five working days between scan and results are much harder)
key_findings.geography: Scanxiety study (56% North America, 33% UK); Dutch quote = Netherlands

key_findings.finding: Metastatic patients cannot make ordinary plans because every horizon is contingent on the next scan; life shrinks to short conditional windows and decisions like quitting work get framed against survival statistics.
key_findings.evidence: "You can't plan ahead because you don't know what is gonna happen to the next scans." (Kathy, UK); "do I do that on the basis that the stats tell me I'll probably be dead..." (Robyn, UK); "The average life expectancy is three years, so I have had two of those years already, does that mean that I'm going to die next year?" (Holly, UK)

key_findings.finding: Living with metastatic cancer is described as a full-time job of ongoing, indefinite treatment layered on top of normal life duties (kids, mortgage, income); treatment is not an interruption but the permanent backdrop.
key_findings.evidence: "if you're living with metastatic cancer, you're living from treatment to treatment, from scan to scan"; "I have to be on some type of treatment to keep that cancer at bay so that it doesn't grow"; "Life doesn't stop when you get diagnosed with cancer. I have a family to take care of" (Jamil Rivers)

key_findings.finding: Long-term metastatic patients run on a rationed-energy economy and develop deliberate emotional-compartmentalization routines to function day to day around family.
key_findings.evidence: "I function like a second-rate cell phone. When it has just been charged, it's fine for a short time, but then the batteries run down."; "I entered the grief room when my boys were at school... But once I saw the boys come through the door, I put on my smile... and went into the joy room." (metastatic GIST patients, mean 6 years on treatment)

key_findings.finding: Daily metastatic coping crystallizes into a concrete maintenance script: take the tablets, attend appointments, treat each new ache pragmatically rather than catastrophically, and protect time for things that bring joy in between.
key_findings.evidence: "Take your tablets, turn up for appointments, and between those times find things that make you happy." (Leapfrog); "Yes, I still worry over every new ache and pain, but take a pain pill and get on with my life." (NMJanet); "You will be surprised at how quickly you adapt and build your life around it." (Dita)

key_findings.finding: The care-circle burden is large and sustained, not episodic: in a Dutch advanced-cancer study, informal caregivers gave a median of 15 hours/week, with 11% reporting high burden, alongside coordinating appointments, meds, and household.
key_findings.evidence: "The eQuiPe study involved 746 relatives of advanced cancer patients in the Netherlands, where 54% reported being informal caregivers with a median of 15 hours of caregiving per week, and 11% experienced high caregiver burden."

key_findings.finding: Scan-result waiting drives concrete avoidant behaviors with real-life cost: not making plans, social withdrawal, dropped chores, and delaying the very appointments that would resolve the uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: "I will not be making plans until I know whether I get to have my next 3 months"; "I disappear for a while to deal with my emotions"; "sink filled with dirty dishes that I didn't do"; study noted "delayed health care appointments for scan results"

key_findings.finding: Even in long-term remission, metastatic patients live with existential dread of drug resistance, and the day-to-day mental task is suppression of negative thought rather than any practical problem.
key_findings.evidence: "The thought of drug resistance is the same as thinking about death."; "The most difficult thing is keeping negative thoughts at bay." (metastatic GIST, long-term remission)

key_findings.finding: Metastatic patients describe a contraction of life-world from participant to spectator, with social and physical reach shrinking markedly.
key_findings.evidence: "I feel like [my life] has shrunk, it was very expansive before and now, it's just tiny, I barely walk up the road..." (Abby, UK); "I feel now that I just look at the world. I watch others rather than participate." (Mary, UK)

surprises: The end of treatment is repeatedly described as harder than treatment itself. The crash often peaks the month after the last infusion, and the loss of the three-weekly hospital rhythm produces an emotional fallout precisely when the support network is celebrating and disappearing. Weekly support is arguably most needed in the phase where it most evaporates.

Fast responsiveness from the care system reads as a danger signal during limbo: a quick hospital callback scared patients into assuming the worst. This inverts the usual product assumption that faster = better; communication framing matters more than speed.

Scanxiety does not habituate. A patient at their 86th scan still gets it, and survivors 17+ years out still feel it. This is a recurring, lifelong trigger event, not a one-time onboarding moment, which fits a persistent companion far better than a one-off summary tool.

The 'gratitude burden' actively suppresses help-seeking: survivors feel ungrateful voicing distress, so the people who most need weekly support are the least likely to ask for it. A proactive, low-friction check-in (vs. a tool you must open and admit a need to) may be the only way to reach them.

Patients spontaneously describe their own intra-cycle rhythm in calendar terms ('chemo Wednesday, sick till Sunday'; 'rough week / better week / human week'). This rhythm is individual but stable per person, which is highly learnable and a natural anchor for timed, anticipatory weekly support.
gaps_or_caveats: The richest verbatim sources skew US, UK, and Norway. Dutch primary voices were found (kanker.nl, uitgezaaideborstkanker.nl) and one NL caregiver study (eQuiPe), but I did not surface deep NL day-in-the-life patient diaries for the active-treatment and off-week phases specifically. The Dutch context for those two phases is inferred from comparable EU/UK/US material.

The metastatic evidence over-indexes on breast cancer and GIST (the segments that blog and study most). Oncology-beachhead-relevant solid tumors with rougher trajectories (lung, pancreatic, ovarian) are thinner on multi-year 'daily texture' because median survival is shorter and patients write less; treat the 'living for years scan-to-scan' picture as most valid for indolent/treatable metastatic disease.

Two strong-looking primary sources (CURE 'Waiting Is the Hardest Part' essay; Inspire ovarian limbo forum thread) returned 403/forbidden and could not be fetched; the limbo-phase patient-voice texture leans on the Norway study and the Dutch kanker.nl blog instead.
Quantitative caregiver figures (15 hrs/week median, 11% high burden) came via search summary of the eQuiPe paper, not a direct fetch of the source; verify the exact numbers before citing externally.

'Weekly support' is not directly defined by patients in these sources. The phase-specific support implications (anticipatory pre-scan check-ins, post-treatment safety-net replacement, intra-cycle crash-day prep) are my synthesis of what the verbatims imply, not claims patients made about a product.

key_findings.finding: The pre-AI baseline is precise: a 2024 scoping review of 525,824 participants found a median ~70% abandonment rate within the first 100 days for lifestyle/mental-health apps, with sharper drop-off right after install then a slowing curve.
key_findings.evidence: "over half of the users discontinued app use within the first 100 days, with a median abandonment rate of approximately 70%" from 18 studies, 525,824 participants, 2014-2022

key_findings.finding: Youper (AI mental-health chatbot) showed a measurably better retention curve than the pre-AI baseline: 90.75% active week 1, 60.44% week 2, 51.78% week 3, 42.66% week 4 among 4,517 paying subscribers.

Youper engagement frontloads sharply then thins: users averaged 6.50 conversations in week 1 falling to 2.04 by week 4 (mean 13.98 over the 4 weeks) - the daily-touch promise decays to roughly twice-a-week within a month.
key_findings.evidence: "Week 1: 6.50 conversations... Week 4: 2.04 conversations... users engaged in an average of 13.98 conversations (SD 16.89)"

key_findings.finding: The general mental-health-app industry comparator is brutally low: across 93 apps, median daily open rate was 4.0%, 15-day retention 3.9%, 30-day retention 3.3% - so any double-digit week-4 retention is an order of magnitude better.
key_findings.evidence: "median 4.0%" daily open rate; "15-day... median 3.9%"; "30-day... median 3.3%" across 93 apps with median 100,000 installs

key_findings.finding: Wysa (AI mental-health) chronic-pain trial hit 70% 30-day retention and a median 51-day retention period, with 20% still engaged past the 8-week study - but this is vendor-affiliated research with no control group.
key_findings.evidence: "30-day retention rate: 70%"; "median user retention period... of 51 days"; "20% of users remained engaged beyond the 8-week study"; 2 of 3 authors hold Wysa equity

key_findings.finding: A morning daily-check-in feature was the single biggest retention driver in the Wysa trial (hazard ratio 0.89, p=.001) - direct evidence that a daily ritual hook, not content volume, extends engagement.
key_findings.evidence: "Morning check-in feature usage significantly extended retention (hazard ratio=0.89, P=.001)"

key_findings.finding: In real-world large-N Wysa data, engagement is far thinner than trials suggest: 4,541 COVID-era users averaged 18.85 sessions (median 13) and ~29 conversations over 15 days - heavy frontloading, long tail.
key_findings.evidence: "Mean sessions: 18.85 per user... Median sessions: 13.00"; over 15 days "an average of 29 conversations and interventions"; n=4,541

key_findings.finding: Woebot's RCT showed near-daily use during a 2-week window: mean 12.14 sessions across ~12 unique days, with only 9% attrition in the Woebot arm vs 31% in the information-only control.
key_findings.evidence: "average of 12.14 (SD 2.23) times over the study period"; "almost all check-ins occurring on unique days"; "Woebot condition had 9% attrition while the control group experienced 31%"; n=70

key_findings.finding: Woebot postpartum RCT (n=184) saw lower-cadence engagement: participants averaged nearly 5 interactions per week, not daily - cadence varies sharply by population and life-stage.
key_findings.evidence: "participants averaging nearly five interactions per week"; 184 participants within 6 months of childbirth

key_findings.finding: Replika (AI companion) is the clearest AI-era retention outlier on the downside, settling near ~20% retention at 90 days despite 40M+ installs and ~14 min average daily use - large reach, weak long-tail stickiness.
key_findings.evidence: "Replika's user retention rate is approximately 20% after 90 days"; "14 minutes of average daily use"; "40 million-plus by 2025"

key_findings.finding: Character.AI represents the AI-era engagement ceiling: ~93 minutes average daily use (Sensor Tower, Sept 2024) and ~17-18 min per session - roughly 8x ChatGPT and longer than TikTok.
key_findings.evidence: "the average user on Character.AI spent 93 minutes a day... according to global data from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower"; "17 minutes and 23 seconds per session"

key_findings.finding: AI companions show a consistent week-three engagement plateau/drop-off across architectures, with survivors past ~10 weeks settling into ~6.1 sessions/week routine use - a recognizable curve shape, not a flat line.
key_findings.evidence: "two to three weeks of high engagement, then a measurable dip between weeks six and ten... users who pass the ten-week mark tend to settle into routine use averaging 6.1 sessions per week"

key_findings.finding: ChatGPT health use is the largest signal of daily-touch behavior, but it is task-driven not relationship-driven: 40M+ people ask health questions daily and ~1 in 4 of 800M weekly users asks a health prompt each week (~200M).
key_findings.evidence: "More than 40 million people ask ChatGPT healthcare questions every day" (OpenAI report, Jan 6 2026); "1 in 4 submits a prompt about healthcare every week"

key_findings.finding: Slingshot's Ash (AI built for therapy) real-world study (n=305, 10 weeks, NYU) reported 75% of users said Ash 'came to mind when they felt distressed' - an internalization/top-of-mind metric, but the study disclosed NO session frequency, retention curve, or daily-use data.
key_findings.evidence: "75% of users reported that Ash came to mind when they felt distressed"; "305 participants"; "47% who didn't complete all assessments"; no sessions/week or retention disclosed

key_findings.finding: Belong.Life's Dave (AI oncology mentor, closest analog to Ditto's space) claims 'exceptionally high engagement' across hundreds of thousands of cancer patients but discloses NO named engagement/retention numbers - only 91.8% clinician-validation of responses.
key_findings.evidence: "hundreds of thousands of cancer patients... exceptionally high levels of engagement"; "432 out of 471... (91.8%) received positive validation"; no usage frequency disclosed

key_findings.finding: Limbic (AI mental-health, NHS) shows AI reduces drop-out in clinical pathways: patients referred via Limbic Access were less likely to drop out, and Limbic Care users attended 42% more sessions with 25% higher recovery vs historical comparators.
key_findings.evidence: "less likely to drop out of treatment"; "patients supported by the tool attended 42% more sessions and showed 25% higher recovery rates" (JMIR Jan 2025)

key_findings.finding: AI journaling apps (Rosebud, Mindsera, Stoic) disclose almost no engagement numbers - only scale signals (Mindsera ~80,000 users; Rosebud '3M+ words journaled') and anecdotal streaks (one user 110-day streak), making this category a data gap.
key_findings.evidence: "Mindsera has 80,000 users"; Rosebud "Over 3 million words journaled"; "one user maintaining a streak of around 110 days" - no DAU/retention disclosed

key_findings.finding: Wysa at scale reports 6M+ users across 95 countries and 'over half a billion AI chat conversations,' claiming 4x engagement vs business-as-usual - useful for scale framing but vendor-reported and not a retention curve.
key_findings.evidence: "over 6 million people across 95 countries"; "over half a billion AI chat conversations... 4x engagement and 10x access to mental health vs business as usual"

surprises: The single best-documented retention DRIVER across the AI-native studies was not the AI's intelligence or content depth - it was a daily morning check-in ritual (Wysa hazard ratio 0.89, p=.001). The hook is the cadence, not the cleverness.

AI-native therapy products show a SHALLOWER decay curve than pre-AI apps (Youper held 42.66% at week 4 vs the ~3.3% industry 30-day median, a 10x+ gap), but the curve shape is identical: sharp frontload then steep drop. AI raises the floor and ceiling but has not flattened the curve.

Slingshot's Ash, a $93M-raised a16z-backed product explicitly built around 'healthy disengagement,' deliberately frames users LEAVING as success ('users naturally disengaged after improvement') - the opposite of a daily-companion retention thesis, and a warning that 'therapeutic' goals can be anti-retention by design.

Character.AI's ~93 min/day blows past every health app and even TikTok - proving AI companions CAN achieve obsessive daily engagement, but it comes from para-social entertainment, not health utility. The engagement is real; the question is whether a care companion can borrow the mechanic without the para-social hook.

The closest direct analog to Ditto (Belong.Life's Dave, AI oncology mentor) publishes zero hard engagement numbers despite years of operation and being the obvious benchmark - suggesting either the numbers aren't flattering or the category genuinely lacks published daily-touch retention data.

ChatGPT is quietly the largest daily-touch health product in existence (40M+ daily health users) and it has no streaks, no check-ins, no companion persona - pure on-demand utility. This challenges the assumption that a care companion needs engineered daily rituals to earn daily return.
gaps_or_caveats: Almost all named retention numbers are from MENTAL-HEALTH AI (Wysa, Youper, Woebot, Ash, Limbic), not chronic-illness or cancer companions. The cancer-specific analogs (Belong.Life Dave, Livestrong Ellis, Kin, Hedy) disclose NO named engagement/retention figures - this is the central data gap for Ditto's exact use case.
Geography skews heavily US plus UK/India (Wysa). No NL/EU-specific AI daily-health-companion retention data was found. Limbic (UK/NHS) is the closest EU signal.

Most AI-vendor figures are self-reported and from single-arm or observational studies with no control group (Youper, Wysa, Ash, Limbic Care). Truly independent app-analytics retention (Sensor Tower/Apptopia) exists mainly for consumer companions (Replika, Character.AI), not clinical tools.

The Replika ~20% 90-day, Character.AI 50-60% D1 / 13-18% D30, and 'week-three plateau' figures come from secondary aggregator blogs, not primary Sensor Tower exports - confidence is low and exact methodology is unverified. Treat as directional.

Engagement metrics are not standardized across studies: 'sessions,' 'conversations,' 'check-ins,' 'interactions,' and 'days active' are used interchangeably, so cross-product comparison of cadence is approximate, not apples-to-apples.

No study isolated whether the AI/LLM layer itself (vs the daily-ritual UX) caused better retention. The pre-AI vs AI-era comparison conflates product era with product design - a confounder the synthesis pipeline should flag rather than treat as causal proof that 'AI improves retention.'

I could not retrieve the underlying Slingshot Ash preprint or the Replika arxiv app-update study text (PDF parse/403 failures), so internalization and companion-bond figures rest on secondary summaries.

key_findings.finding: Acoustic voice biomarkers add little to nothing over transcribed words: for depression and PTSD classification, audio+text actually UNDERPERFORMED text-only by ~2-4% across the best LLMs.
key_findings.evidence: Text-only best Deepseek_R1 79.8% BA / 0.78 F1 vs audio+text best Gemini 2.5 Pro 77.8% BA / 0.77 F1; PTSD text-only 77% BA vs audio+text 73.6% BA, '~3-4% degradation'. 'acoustic voice characteristics did not reliably enhance classification beyond what transcribed language provided.'

key_findings.finding: Kintsugi, the highest-profile voice-biomarker depression company, shut down commercial operations in Feb 2026 after raising ~$28-30M, citing FDA cost/timeline and a distressed market (it open-sourced its tech rather than failing on science alone).
key_findings.evidence: 'Mental Health Voice Biomarker Kintsugi Closes, Makes All Technology and Research Public'; 'the high cost and lengthy timeline of FDA regulatory hurdles ultimately made the venture-backed business model unsustainable'; 'chose the integrity of the science over the limitations of a distressed market.'

key_findings.finding: Kintsugi's largest independent validation hit only 71.3% sensitivity / 73.5% specificity for moderate-severe depression, far below its marketed '80% accuracy', with a severe gender bias (men 59.3% sensitivity vs women 74.0%).
key_findings.evidence: Sensitivity 71.3% (95% CI 69.0-73.5), specificity 73.5%; 'Sensitivity for men was 59.3% versus 74.0% for women'; validation set 4,456 of 14,898 enrolled; AUC not reported.

key_findings.finding: The most directly on-point oncology-adjacent test of talk-instead-of-type largely FAILED: extracting palliative-care symptoms (IPOS) from conversational voice scored all F1 below 0.5, and patient speech transcribed at only 55.6% accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: F1: anxiety 0.46, depression 0.45, feeling-at-peace 0.43, pain 0.36, practical matters 0.31 (all <0.5); patient-speech transcription 55.6% (SD 12.1%) vs provider 82.2%; 'still requires further improvements to be applied in clinical practice.'

key_findings.finding: The high LLM symptom-extraction accuracy people cite (GPT-4 F1 ~91-94%) is from clean PHYSICIAN clinical notes, not patient natural speech, so it does not transfer to a voice-diary product.
key_findings.evidence: GPT-4 F1 91.4% (test) / 94.0% (validation) vs ICD-10 45.1%; 11 symptoms; 'Data source: Physician notes from emergency departments, not patient-generated speech.'

key_findings.finding: Dutch ASR for elderly speakers is poor out-of-the-box: Whisper hits 28.73% word error rate on native elderly Dutch (42% for non-native adults), only dropping to ~9% after fine-tuning on the JASMIN-CGN corpus.
key_findings.evidence: 'Whisper achieved a WER of 28.73% on native elderly Dutch speech and 42.07% on non-native adult speech'; after fine-tuning: elderly 9.11%, non-native 14.01%.

key_findings.finding: Voice-biomarker validation overall is a field-wide translation failure: across systematic reviews only 1 of 89 (and 1 of 308) models was ever considered for clinical implementation, with diagnostic accuracy ranging wildly from 21% to 100%.
key_findings.evidence: 'out of 89 models included in the review...one was considered for implementation'; 'out of 308 models, one had its potential utility formally assessed'; 'diagnostic accuracy ranges from 21% to 100%'; '94% of published studies on depression involve fewer than 100 participants.'

key_findings.finding: Dutch hospitals already run voice-to-structured-report in the consultation room (mProve / Jeroen Bosch Ziekenhuis), transcribing the doctor-patient conversation and auto-summarizing side effects, with clinician review before the record. This is doctor-led capture, not patient self-tracking.
key_findings.evidence: 'Six top clinical hospitals in the Netherlands use voice-guided AI solutions'; system 'used to discuss with patients how they are doing and especially whether prescribed medications have side effects'; 'an algorithm then generates a summary, which clinicians review before adding to the electronic patient record'; patients can opt out.

key_findings.finding: Sonde Health's voice biomarker is explicitly positioned as a 'mental wellbeing thermometer,' not diagnostic; it only reaches a meaningful signal when AGGREGATED over weeks and falls apart with single samples or low engagement.
key_findings.evidence: Relative Risk 2.00 (1.21-3.30) aggregated over 2 weeks; single voice samples RR only 1.53; low-engagement group RR <1.0; authors: 'not a diagnostic or screening instrument' but a 'mental wellbeing thermometer'; anxiety/PTSD 'inconsistent... non-significant.' n=104, Pittsburgh.

key_findings.finding: Voice biomarkers generalize poorly across language/culture, which directly threatens any Dutch deployment trained on English data: a cognitive-impairment study saw 23% speech-metric variation in the Indian cohort vs only 4% in the US cohort.
key_findings.evidence: '23% variation in the Indian and 4% in the US cohort'; cognitive impairment effect 'statistically significant (p<0.01) in India only.' India n=157 (Kerala), US n=57 (Bronx).

key_findings.finding: Canary Speech (cognitive, not symptom) shows the strongest validated voice-biomarker signal of the bunch, detecting mild cognitive impairment from ~3 min of conversation at AUC 0.88-0.89, beating demographics-only models (0.78-0.80).
key_findings.evidence: 'AUC scores of 0.88 and 0.89... outperformed traditional models based only on age, sex, and education (AUCs 0.78-0.80)'; 1,461 adults in Japan, 36% impaired; published in The Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific.

key_findings.finding: Voice biomarkers for chronic pain (highly relevant to oncology) remain early-stage: accuracies scatter 60-85% across only 25 mostly-tiny studies, with the few pain-vocal features failing to reach statistical significance.
key_findings.evidence: 25 studies, accuracy 60-85%; pain vocalizations showed longer durations/increased jitter but 'these features did not reach statistical significance'; mostly 'studies under 100 participants'; 'lack the standardization and validation necessary for reliable clinical deployment.'

key_findings.finding: Voice/automated symptom check-ins in elderly chronic care show modest, soft adherence benefit, not strong evidence: a voice-assistant medication reminder study found 82-100% adherence but median 55-min latency and only 14.6% of doses taken within 5 min of the cue.
key_findings.evidence: Adherence 82-100% across 5 participants; mean latency 55 min (SD 100); within 5 min 14.6% (25/168), within 30 min 63.7%; 'Voice assistant reminders may help cue patients... but the timing of medication use may vary.' n=15, Midwest US.

key_findings.finding: Even FORM-based (not voice) digital symptom monitoring in real-world oncology struggles with sustained engagement: a German metastatic-NSCLC pilot saw 85% access once but 32% premature discontinuation and only 38% completing the separate PRO questionnaires.
key_findings.evidence: 85.1% accessed Kaiku Health at least once; 31.9% (15/47) prematurely discontinued; 'Only 38.3% submitted PRO questionnaires'; recruited only 47 of 100 planned over 17 months; input was form-based, no voice.

key_findings.finding: For zero-shot symptom/mood extraction from patient text, top open and closed LLMs already exceed 90% F1/accuracy, confirming the language-content path is the strong one (vs acoustics).
key_findings.evidence: 'Three out of five LLMs demonstrated... over 90% of F-1 and accuracy, with Llama 3.1 405B achieving 93%' for depression/anxiety from patient messages (zero-shot).

key_findings.finding: A 2024 review found voice biomarkers underperform the cheap PHQ-9 form they aim to replace, and depression-specificity of vocal features has never been systematically established.
key_findings.evidence: 'A 2024 review found that the efficacy of vocal biomarkers as indicators for depression is below that of the PHQ-9 form'; 'the degree to which changes in vocal features are specific to depression has not been systematically studied'; Lancet editorial: 'still a long way to go before AI-powered vocal biomarkers can be endorsed by the clinical community.'

surprises: The signal lives in WORDS, not VOICE. Multiple LLM studies show audio biomarkers add ~0% (or hurt by 2-4%) over the transcript. The entire 'voice biomarker' acoustic premise (prosody, pitch, jitter) is largely a distraction for symptom/mood capture; the leverage is ASR + LLM on what the patient actually says. This collapses the build decision from 'do we need a voice-biomarker partner' to 'do we need good Dutch ASR plus an LLM extractor.'

Kintsugi, the category's flagship and FDA-De-Novo-pathway leader, is DEAD as of Feb 2026 and gave its IP away. The single most-cited proof point for 'voice-based mental health works as a product' is now a cautionary tale about regulatory cost killing the business model.

The one study that tested exactly Ditto's use case (extract oncology/palliative symptoms from conversational patient speech) failed across the board (all F1 <0.5), and the failure was driven by patient-speech transcription collapsing to 55.6% accuracy. Sick, tired, soft-spoken patients are the hardest ASR population, the opposite of the clean speech these models are trained on.

Dutch elderly speech breaks general ASR (28.7% WER with Whisper). A 28% word error rate means roughly 1 in 4 words wrong before any symptom logic runs. Fine-tuning fixes it (~9%) but that requires a Dutch elderly/patient speech corpus Ditto would have to build or license.

The genuinely strong, reproducible voice signal is for COGNITIVE decline (Canary Speech AUC ~0.88), not for mood/symptom/medication capture. The validated science points at a different problem than the one being scoped.
gaps_or_caveats: No found study tested LLM symptom/mood extraction from patient natural SPEECH in DUTCH specifically. The Dutch evidence is ASR word-error-rate only (JASMIN-CGN); the symptom-extraction evidence is all English/clinical-text. The combined Dutch-patient-speech-to-symptom pipeline is unvalidated.

Vendor-reported numbers (Sonde 'accurately identifies', Canary 'detect Alzheimer's in 40 seconds') are PR framing; the peer-reviewed versions are consistently weaker and hedged (risk ratios, 'thermometer not diagnostic', interim findings). Treat any single marketed accuracy figure as a ceiling, not an expectation.

Almost no head-to-head adherence/engagement data exists for VOICE check-ins vs typed/tapped forms in oncology specifically. The adherence numbers found are from tiny elderly-pain feasibility studies (n=5-15) or form-based oncology pilots, none isolating the talk-vs-type variable that Ditto cares about.

Kintsugi's shutdown reason is contested: company PR frames it as FDA cost + market, not science. The independent evidence (71% sensitivity, gender bias) suggests the science was also marginal, but I could not find a clean published statement attributing closure to efficacy failure.

The Canary Speech MCI AUC 0.88-0.89 (Lancet) is reported via the company blog/press, not read from the primary Lancet paper directly; confidence is medium pending the journal source. The separately fetched US/India cognitive study is independent (Alzheimer's & Dementia), not Canary, and showed poor cross-culture generalization.

Most validation samples are US, female-skewed, white-skewed, and English. Generalization to a Dutch oncology population (older, sicker, mixed L1, often soft/fatigued voices) is the single biggest unproven risk and the cross-culture data (23% vs 4% variation) suggests it will degrade meaningfully.

key_findings.finding: Hinge Health identified an early 'habit point': members who complete six exercise-therapy sessions in the first two weeks are far more likely to stick long-term, defining the activation window for a daily/near-daily companion.
key_findings.evidence: members who complete six exercise therapy sessions in the first two weeks are more likely to reach a 'habit point' and stick to the program long-term, as well as experience greater initial pain relief as a result (5th annual State of MSK Care Report, Jan 2025)

key_findings.finding: Hinge Health's 1-on-1 coaching drove a 73% 12-week completion rate with an average of 35 exercise-therapy sessions completed per participant (roughly 3 per week over 12 weeks), the cadence that produced their best outcomes.
key_findings.evidence: 1-on-1 coaching model helped drive the industry's highest 12-week completion rate, 73%, with each participant completing an average of 35 exercise therapy sessions

key_findings.finding: Sword Health sustains an 81% care-completion rate (about double the ~50% in-person dropout), and notably 42% of sessions happen outside the workday and 23% on weekends, suggesting check-ins must fit the user's own rhythm rather than impose a fixed clinic-style schedule.
key_findings.evidence: 81% adherence rate ... 42% of sessions happen outside the standard workday, and 23% on weekends ... more than 50% of patients quit after just four sessions [in traditional PT]

key_findings.finding: Virta achieves 83% retention at 1 year and 74% at 2 years in type-2 diabetes, attributed substantially to daily biomarker logging that returns immediate self-tracked feedback multiple times a day, not just periodic coaching.
key_findings.evidence: retention rates of 83% at one year and 74% at two years ... daily biomarkers from blood glucose and blood ketones provide feedback multiple times a day ... immediate feedback from their biomarkers and their health coach

key_findings.finding: Virta's own breakdown of why it retains lists 'quick results,' 'daily feedback & empowerment,' 'sustainability,' and 'proactive outreach' via software (Spark) that flags at-risk patients so clinicians reach out at the right time, i.e. proactivity is system-triggered, not on a fixed calendar.
key_findings.evidence: Virta uses a proprietary software, Spark, to inform clinicians who is at risk ... reach out to patients at the right time ... patients track their biomarkers daily, and they're able to get immediate feedback

key_findings.finding: Livongo's model is the cleanest example of automatic reciprocity: members checked glucose ~1.8x/day and every check triggered an immediate two-way message back, with the explicit design goal of being present 'at the decision point.'
key_findings.evidence: members using the Livongo glucose meter to measure their BG levels an average of 1.8 times per day ... delivers messages back to the individual in real time ... there at the decision point to nudge the person if blood glucose strays out of range

key_findings.finding: In Noom's engagement study (N=11,252), weigh-ins were the single most predictive engagement behavior for weight loss (adjusted R2=0.17), narrowly ahead of meal logging (0.16); the highest-loss users weighed in only once per week, not daily.
key_findings.evidence: Weigh-ins: adjusted R2 = 0.17 at 9-16 weeks; Meals logged: adjusted R2 = 0.16 ... high weight loss group: Logged 24 meals per week ... Weighed in once per week ... Messaged coach once every 2 weeks (N=11,252)

key_findings.finding: Noom engagement decays across nearly all behaviors over 52 weeks, yet the gap between engaged and disengaged users on outcomes persists even as absolute engagement falls, suggesting early intensity matters more than sustaining peak frequency.
key_findings.evidence: means of the following engagement measures decreased over time across all weight groups: days with at least 1 meal logged, articles read ... differences between each weight loss category and stable weight were maintained even as engagement decreased over time

key_findings.finding: Noom's dose-response is concrete: at week 40 the top engagement quartile lost 8.3 lbs more (about 25% more) than the bottom quartile, and 77.8% of its GLP-1 companion users stayed engaged 4+ weeks, with D30 engagement at 43.6% (~10x typical health-app retention).
key_findings.evidence: At week 40, the difference between the top and bottom quartiles was an additional 8.3 lbs of weight loss—about 25% more weight loss ... At 30 days, 43.6% of users engaged with the app ... nearly 80% (77.8%) of all Microdose GLP-1Rx users stayed engaged ... for 4 or more weeks

key_findings.finding: Omada's 3-year data shows voluntary engagement (logins + group participation) was the only factor predicting weight loss, while passive lesson completion alone did not predict outcomes once other behaviors were controlled, arguing reciprocal/social check-ins beat content consumption.
key_findings.evidence: Only the logins and group participation factor was a significant predictor of weight loss ... neither the present study nor those studies just cited have identified online lesson module completion as a significant predictor of weight loss once other program behaviors ... had been taken into account

key_findings.finding: Omada engagement and data submission decline steeply after the structured curriculum ends: weight-measurement participation fell from 73% at 1yr to 66% at 2yr to 46% at 3yr once active coaching and weekly curriculum stopped, a warning that removing structured cadence collapses engagement.
key_findings.evidence: 1 year: 161 participants (73%) ... 2 years: 145 (66%) ... 3 years: 102 (46%) ... engagement was substantially reduced [in years 2-3 due to] lack of continuing curriculum and active coaching

key_findings.finding: Respiratory adherence (Hailie/Propeller smart inhaler) reminders plus tracking drove a 59% increase in controller-medication adherence in adults, an 80% reduction in pediatric hospital admissions, and a 45% reduction in rescue inhaler use, showing scheduled medication check-ins with visible trend feedback work.
key_findings.evidence: a 59% increase in controller medication adherence in adults using the Hailie sensor, an 80% reduction in hospital admissions in children ... 45% reduction in rescue medication use in children

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy apps are the strongest consumer daily-health-habit category because of a built-in weekly anticipation hook (week-by-week baby development and shareable fruit/size comparisons) that gives the user something new and emotionally rewarding each open without any data entry required.
key_findings.evidence: every week right when I open the app there's a comparison to a familiar fruit, so it's easy for me to visualize how big my baby is ... The Bump is described as 'the original home of the cute fruit' ... in a way that's fun and easy to share with friends and family

key_findings.finding: Flo built daily story-format content (WhatsApp/Instagram-style) that lifted app opens 30%+ for freemium users and hit a 61.42% watch rate among 480,000+ pregnant women, plus a self-reinforcing data loop where logging improves predictions, so the user gets a sharper personalized payoff each time they log.
key_findings.evidence: daily content in a story format ... saw a 30%+ increase in app opens, with the content deployed to over 480,000+ pregnant women achieving a 61.42% watch rate ... the more a woman uses Flo, the more it can accurately guide her
key_findings.geography: Global (Flo HQ in EU/Lithuania, US user base)

key_findings.finding: Practitioner synthesis of health-app retention says the daily loop must be tiny (under 60 seconds, ideally 30 seconds) with an immediate reward (streak count or health insight), capped at 2 notifications/day, and that an accountability partner yields 2-3x higher 90-day retention.
key_findings.evidence: make the desired behavior tiny (30-second daily check-in vs 45-minute workout) ... immediate reward (streak count, health insight) ... Maximum 2 notifications per day ... Users with an accountability partner have 2-3x higher 90-day retention

key_findings.finding: The same source pins the month-3 cliff: AI/automated nudges retain well only 30-60 days, and beyond month 3 (3-12 months) human accountability coaches significantly outperform pure-app retention, against an average D90 of just 6-10% (top fitness apps 15-20%).
key_findings.evidence: AI and automated nudges retain well for 30-60 days ... For long-term habit change (3-12 months), human accountability coaches significantly outperform pure-app retention ... D90 performance drops to 6-10% for average apps

key_findings.finding: Proactive coaching beats reactive coaching on engagement with hard numbers: proactive/personalized coaching produced 19.37 vs 8.55 coach messages and 49.31 vs 40.06 app-open days, though the 16-week weight-loss difference (10.1% vs 8.9%) was not statistically significant.
key_findings.evidence: the proactive group sent an average of 19.37 messages compared to 8.55 in the reactive group, and opened the app an average of 49.31 days versus 40.06 days ... 16-week weight loss was 10.1% in the proactive group compared to 8.9% ... not statistically significant

key_findings.finding: Streaks backfire badly in emotionally sensitive health contexts: only 0.90% of users who lose a 2-3 day streak return to rebuild it (1.42% for a 4-7 day streak), so punitive streak mechanics risk total abandonment after the first miss for cancer patients.
key_findings.evidence: Only 0.90% of users who lose a streak of two to three days return to rebuild it, and for users who lose a streak of four to seven days, the figure is 1.42% ... a break can feel like failure

key_findings.finding: Foundational habit science (Lally/UCL, N=96 over 12 weeks) found automaticity takes a median 66 days (range 18-254), simpler behaviors form fastest (water before breakfast ~18-20 days), and crucially 'missing a single day did not reduce the chance of forming a habit' - direct evidence against perfection-based streaks.
key_findings.evidence: it takes an average of 66 days for a new behavior to become automatic ... from 18 days at the fast end to 254 days at the slow end ... Missing a single day did not reduce the chance of forming a habit

key_findings.finding: CGM/real-time biofeedback works because feedback is instantaneous: a meta-analysis of 25 RCTs found CGM-based feedback reduced HbA1c by 0.28% and increased time-in-range by 7.4%, attributed to immediate feedback raising the likelihood the user acts in the moment.
key_findings.evidence: Interventions incorporating CGM-based feedback reduced HbA1c by 0.28% and increased time in range by 7.4% ... the instantaneous feedback increases the likelihood that patients will take action

key_findings.finding: Wearable daily-habit products (Oura, Whoop) anchor the open to a single morning reward delivered with zero input: a color-coded readiness/recovery score plus a strain target, available immediately on waking - the no-friction reciprocity that a passive daily companion could mimic.
key_findings.evidence: both devices provide users with a color-coded verdict on how their body is doing each morning ... Oura Ring provides sleep and readiness scores almost immediately upon waking ... Whoop gives users a Recovery percentage each morning, plus a Target Strain for the day ... Oura ... doesn't require users to log anything

surprises: Weigh-ins, not meal logging or coach messages, were Noom's single most predictive engagement behavior (R2=0.17), and the highest-loss users weighed in only once a week - evidence that the most powerful check-in may be a low-frequency self-measurement, not a daily one.

Across Noom, Omada and Hinge, engagement DECLINES over time for everyone, yet the gap between engaged and disengaged users on outcomes persists. This reframes the goal: don't fight inevitable decay, front-load intensity in the first two weeks to clear the 'habit point.'

The pregnancy-app daily hook requires zero data entry - the reciprocity is delivered content (this week your baby is the size of a lime), not feedback on logged data. This is the opposite of the diabetes/MSK 'log-then-get-feedback' loop and may be the better model for emotionally exhausted cancer patients.

Lally's canonical habit research directly contradicts streak design: missing one day did not hurt habit formation, while real streak data shows <1% of users return after breaking a 2-3 day streak. Punitive streaks may actively destroy the habit they claim to build.

Proactive coaching produced more than 2x the coach messages and meaningfully more app-open days than reactive coaching, but did NOT produce statistically significant better weight loss at 16 weeks - proactivity drives engagement metrics more reliably than it drives the clinical outcome.

Omada's lesson completion (passive content consumption) did not predict outcomes once social participation and logins were controlled - a caution that an AI companion serving educational content without a reciprocal/social loop may generate vanity engagement.
gaps_or_caveats: Almost all retention disclosures (Sword, Hinge, Virta, Omada, Noom, Livongo) are US-based and run inside employer/payer-sponsored programs, where the user did not pay and often has an external incentive. EU/NL consumer-pay daily-habit benchmarks are thin; pregnancy apps (Flo is EU-HQ'd) are the closest consumer analogue but publish marketing metrics, not audited retention curves.

Company-published retention figures (Sword '100% client retention,' Hinge '98% client retention') are CLIENT/enterprise retention, not individual-user daily-engagement retention - they say nothing about whether an individual still opens the app at month 3. Treat these as commercial, not behavioral, metrics.

Almost none of these products are a pure daily companion; they bundle hardware (CGM, smart inhaler, motion sensors) or a structured clinical curriculum. The reciprocity often comes from a device returning real data, which a software-only cancer companion cannot replicate without an equivalent 'new information each day' source.

No source gave a clean, isolated month-3 individual retention number for a software-only daily check-in; the strongest month-3 evidence (productgrowth synthesis) is a practitioner blog, not peer-reviewed, so its specific numbers should be treated as medium-confidence directional guidance.

Cancer-specific daily/weekly companion engagement data was not found in this pass - all findings are transferred from MSK, diabetes, respiratory, weight-loss and pregnancy. The emotional load and unpredictable, episodic burden of cancer (treatment weeks vs recovery weeks) may break the fixed-cadence assumptions that work in chronic metabolic disease.

Streak-backfire return rates (0.90% / 1.42%) come from a single vendor blog citing aggregate app data without methodology; directionally consistent with Lally but should be verified before being used as a hard design constraint.
The arxiv fitness habit-formation study (2501.01779) could not be parsed in this pass, so its specific cadence/phase thresholds are unverified - only Lally's 66-day finding is confirmed.

uncovered_hours: MISSING 10th AGENT / CAREGIVER DAY: The brief says '10-agent sweep' but only 9 missions are shown, and none reconstruct the care-circle member's hour-by-hour week. Two agents flag this explicitly (day-reconstruction gap: 'I did not separately reconstruct the caregiver's day... core to Ditto's growth thesis'; nl-voices: 'partner reaches moments of being unable to even listen'). We have caregiver TIME aggregates (33h/wk US; 15h/wk median NL eQuiPe; ~66h/wk in last year of life) but ZERO clock-hour texture: what does the caregiver do at 7am, during the 6-8h infusion wait, on a crash evening, on a near-normal day? For a product whose growth engine IS the care circle, the entire B-side of every day is a hole.

THE 'NEAR-NORMAL' WEEK (days 14-20 of a 21-day cycle): Every week-mission narrates the crash (days 3-5) in rich texture but treats the recovery/near-normal week as a single phrase ('feels near-complete by day 7', 'near-normal week before next infusion'). We cannot account for the hours of a GOOD day mid-cycle: does the patient work? Exercise? Catch up on the admin backlog? Have sex? This is precisely the window a daily companion must earn its keep in — if there is no symptom to manage, what is the daily hook? Explicitly flagged: emotional-cycle gap ('the ordinary Tuesday of someone mid-treatment but not blogging is under-represented'); phase-contrast gap ('did not surface deep NL day-in-the-life for active-treatment and off-week phases specifically').

WEEKEND vs WEEKDAY STRUCTURE: All day-reconstruction is implicitly weekday-shaped (clinic access, work calendar, school run, no-early-calls). No agent isolates how Saturday/Sunday differ — when clinic/helpline is closed, partner is home all day, kids have no school anchor, and the 'is this normal / should I worry' channel (named as a distinct unmet need in phase-contrast) is unavailable. The check-in-design evidence even shows 42% of Sword sessions are outside workday and 23% on weekends, so weekend rhythm is a live product variable that lived-reality coverage never touched.

THE 3am-to-7am DEAD ZONE, AWAKE: Multiple agents establish patients are AWAKE at night (steroid insomnia ~45%, 3-4h sleep ceiling, midnight/3am vomiting, actigraphy shows MORE activity at night during chemo, 'fill the small hours with quiet busywork', night = hardest emotional window for rumination). But what the patient actually DOES in those waking small hours hour-by-hour — beyond 'cleaning' and 'rumination' — is thin. This is the single most product-relevant uncovered window: a daily AI companion's strongest theoretical wedge is the 3am awake-and-afraid hour, yet we have almost no texture on what would actually be wanted then vs. resented.

ORAL-THERAPY / NON-INFUSION REGIMENS: The entire week-reconstruction is built around the IV infusion cycle (infusion day, steroid pre-meds, 21-day shape, take-home pump). Oncology is increasingly oral targeted therapy / daily pills with no infusion-day anchor and a flat-but-grinding daily side-effect profile. Steroid-timing verbatims even over-index on myeloma weekly oral dex (flagged in emotional-cycle gap). The day-shape of a patient on daily oral therapy — no couch-day rhythm, no recovery week, just continuous low-grade — is essentially uncovered, and it may be the fastest-growing segment of Ditto's beachhead.

INTER-APPOINTMENT 'NOTHING SCHEDULED' DAYS: Coverage is dense on appointment/infusion/scan days (the events) and crash days (the symptoms), but the genuinely empty day — no clinic, no crash, no scan looming — is barely textured except as 'normalcy illusion.' For retention modeling this matters: the days with no external trigger are exactly where a daily companion either creates its own reason to open or gets abandoned. We cannot currently say what fills a structurally empty mid-cycle Wednesday.

MEALTIMES AND THE EATING CLOCK on non-crash days: We have rich crash-day eating texture (cold/sweet/frozen foods, smell aversion, scheduled defensive eating) but the eating rhythm of an ordinary on-treatment day — breakfast with kids, whether appetite returns by week 2, family dinner dynamics — is uncovered. Eating is a 3x/day clock event and a natural check-in anchor; we only see it when it is broken.

MEDICATION-ADMINISTRATION CLOCK across the full day: We know fixed alarms trigger meds and patients juggle standing vs as-needed anti-nausea, take up to 20 pills/day, call pharmacy 5+ days out. But the actual within-day medication schedule (morning steroid taper, anti-emetic timing relative to meals, bedtime meds) as a recurring daily-clock structure is fragmentary — and it is the most obvious, lowest-creativity daily companion hook, so its texture is load-bearing for the build decision.
claims_to_verify: EVENING vs MORNING FATIGUE ARE DISTINCT (~80% evening vs ~67% morning; morning oscillates peaking weeks 1&3, evening stays elevated). LOAD-BEARING because it directly dictates check-in TIMING — if true, an evening check-in catches the worse, more persistent state but a morning one catches the only reliably-functional window. SURPRISING because it contradicts the naive 'tired all day' model. Verify the exact Miaskowski cohort percentages, that the morning/evening split is statistically distinct (not just two cutoffs on one scale), and the cycle-week oscillation claim — all flagged as US breast/mixed-tumor, EU-unverified.

MORNING DAILY CHECK-IN WAS THE SINGLE BIGGEST RETENTION DRIVER in the Wysa chronic-pain trial (hazard ratio 0.89, p=.001). This is arguably the most decision-relevant single number in the entire AI corpus — it is the closest thing to direct evidence that the daily-ritual hook (not content) extends engagement. SURPRISING/SUSPECT: HR 0.89 is a SMALL effect, the study is vendor-affiliated with NO control group, and 'morning' here may be an artifact of how the feature was deployed. Verify the HR direction/magnitude, what outcome it predicts, and whether 'morning' is causal or incidental before this anchors any product timing decision.

VOICE/AUDIO ADDS NOTHING OVER TEXT and the on-point oncology test FAILED (palliative IPOS extraction all F1 < 0.5, patient speech transcribed at 55.6% accuracy; audio+text UNDERPERFORMED text-only by 2-4%). LOAD-BEARING because it kills or keeps the 'talk to your companion' modality. SURPRISING because the whole voice-biomarker category was hyped. Verify the IPOS F1<0.5 and 55.6% ASR figures against the primary palliative-care paper, and confirm the audio-underperforms-text result is on patient (not clinician) speech — this single finding could veto a voice-first design.

DUTCH ASR FOR ELDERLY SPEAKERS IS 28.73% WORD ERROR RATE out-of-the-box (Whisper), only dropping to ~9% after JASMIN-CGN fine-tuning. DIRECTLY DECISION-RELEVANT for an NL oncology product whose users are older, fatigued, soft-voiced. Verify the 28.73% figure and that ~9% post-fine-tuning number, because a 29% WER on the actual target population is a build-blocker for any voice input in the home market.

STREAKS BACKFIRE: only 0.90% of users who break a 2-3 day streak return (1.42% for 4-7 day). LOAD-BEARING AND SURPRISING because it inverts the default gamification playbook and is especially damning for cancer patients who WILL miss days during crashes. But the critic flags it comes from 'a single vendor blog citing aggregate app data without methodology.' Verify or replace with a methodologically sound source before it becomes a hard design constraint — currently the strongest anti-streak evidence rests on the weakest source.

REPLIKA SETTLES NEAR ~20% RETENTION AT 90 DAYS despite 40M+ installs and ~14 min/day use; Character.AI ~93 min/day. These bracket the AI-companion retention ceiling and floor and would heavily shape Ditto's retention assumptions. SURPRISING that the highest-engagement AI products still bleed to ~20% at D90. Flagged as coming from 'secondary aggregator blogs, not primary Sensor Tower exports — confidence is low.' Verify against primary app-analytics before using as a planning anchor.

PRE-CHEMO SLEEP SETS THE TONE FOR THE ENTIRE 3-WEEK CYCLE: patients who slept poorly the night before infusion (~55% of sample) reported greater fatigue and more anxious mood ACROSS THE WHOLE CYCLE. LOAD-BEARING because it identifies a specific, single, predictable LEVERAGE POINT (the night before infusion) where a companion intervention could plausibly change the next 21 days — the rare causal-looking, actionable claim. Verify the cohort, the 55% figure, and that the association holds across the full cycle (not just days 1-2).

MEDIAN ~7 HOURS/WEEK (400 min) MANAGING CANCER, with a 2:1 travel-and-wait-to-treatment ratio and 35% of patients reporting disruption on >half of study days. This is the headline quantification of the 'invisible admin job' that justifies an admin-assistant companion surface. SURPRISING in magnitude and the 2:1 ratio. But it is US-only, n=60, metastatic breast + advanced ovarian, 77% White, median age 59 — verify the numbers and ruthlessly check transferability to NL (where prior-auth doesn't exist and the admin structure is entirely different), since the build case for an admin surface partly rests on this single small study.
contradictions: MORNING IS BEST vs MORNING IS WORST. Most missions converge that mid-morning is the 'good window' and afternoon/evening is the dip (day-reconstruction: 'mid-morning is the recommended and lived good window'; emotional-cycle: 'mornings tend to be the better-functioning window'). But cognitive-physical-micro states the opposite: 'Mornings are reported as the worst window of the day, with patients winded within minutes of waking.' This is a direct conflict on the single most product-critical variable (when to check in). Likely reconciled by symptom-type (fatigue/cognition favor morning; breathlessness/physical-deconditioning and acute on-crash-days favor evening) and by treatment phase, but it is currently an unresolved contradiction that any timing decision must adjudicate.

DAILY-TOUCH CADENCE IS THE GOAL vs DAILY CADENCE DECAYS TO ~TWICE-WEEKLY IS NORMAL AND FINE. The checkin-design and companion-retention agents are internally inconsistent: one stream treats a daily ritual as the retention driver (Wysa morning check-in HR; Livongo 1.8x/day; 'daily loop under 60 seconds'), while the same corpus shows the best real-world products settle BELOW daily (Noom's highest-loss users weighed in ONCE A WEEK; Woebot postpartum ~5x/week not daily; Youper decays to 2.04 conversations/week by week 4; survivors plateau at ~6/week). The evidence does not actually support 'daily' as the winning cadence — it supports 'early intensity then a sustainable lower cadence.' This is a contradiction the synthesis must resolve before committing to a DAILY surface specifically.

AI IMPROVES RETENTION vs THE COMPARISON IS CONFOUNDED. companion-retention presents AI products beating the ~70% / 100-day abandonment baseline as if AI is the cause, then its OWN gaps section retracts it: 'No study isolated whether the AI/LLM layer itself (vs the daily-ritual UX) caused better retention... a confounder the pipeline should flag rather than treat as causal.' The headline finding and the caveat directly oppose each other on whether 'build AI' is supported by the retention data.

NAUSEA IS THE DEFINING CRASH SYMPTOM vs STEROIDS (NOT NAUSEA) ARE WHY DAYS 1-2 ARE WORST vs MODERN ANTI-EMETICS MAKE NAUSEA OVERSTATED. day-reconstruction simultaneously holds: clockwork midnight/3am vomiting and a 'puke-or-feel-like-puking baseline' organizing the day; AND 'patients name days 1-2 as their worst specifically because steroids wreck their sleep, not because of nausea'; AND its own gap that improved anti-emetics mean 'older studies may understate nausea' while 'vivid diary accounts may predate current anti-emetic standards.' The actual prevalence and timing of nausea for Ditto's current-regimen users is internally unsettled — it cannot be both the organizing axis of the day and a possibly-dated symptom.

WORST PART IS THE WAITING/LIMBO (pre-treatment) vs WORST PART IS AFTER TREATMENT ENDS (the 'zwarte gat'). phase-contrast: in diagnosis-to-treatment limbo 'the waiting itself, not the treatment, is named as the worst part of the whole process.' nl-voices: 'The hardest part is not treatment but life AFTER it ends: the zwarte gat.' Both are stated as 'the hardest part.' Not necessarily false (different phases, different patients) but presented without reconciliation — and it matters because it points the product's emotional-support emphasis at opposite ends of the journey.

EU PERCENTAGES ARE TRANSFERABLE vs THEY ARE NOT. Across missions the US-derived quantified findings (diurnal fatigue classes, 400 min/week admin, prior-auth time loss) are used as the texture of 'the cancer week,' while every gap section warns they are US-only and structurally non-transferable to NL (different anti-emetics, no prior-auth, eigen-risico/UWV system, JASMIN ASR degradation). The corpus leans on numbers it simultaneously says don't apply to the actual market — a pervasive tension rather than a single clean contradiction.
thinnest_evidence: CANCER-SPECIFIC / CHRONIC-ILLNESS AI COMPANION RETENTION: This is the single thinnest spot relative to the build decision. Every named retention curve is from MENTAL-HEALTH AI (Wysa, Youper, Woebot, Ash, Limbic). The exact analogs — Belong.Life Dave (oncology), Livestrong Ellis, Kin, Hedy — disclose ZERO named engagement/retention numbers. The decision 'build a daily AI companion for cancer' is being made on retention evidence borrowed entirely from a different disease context with a different daily burden profile (cancer's episodic, crash-driven, unpredictable load may break the fixed-cadence assumptions that work in metabolic disease — flagged explicitly). We literally have no retention number for the actual product category.

WHETHER THE 'AI' IS WHAT RETAINS (vs the daily-ritual UX, the reciprocity device, or the human coach). The corpus repeatedly shows the retention wins are attributable to NON-AI mechanics: a fixed morning ritual, a device returning real data (CGM, smart inhaler, glucose), or human accountability coaches (which 'significantly outperform pure-app retention beyond month 3'). The checkin-design gaps note 'none of these products is a pure daily companion; the reciprocity often comes from a device returning real data, which a software-only cancer companion cannot replicate.' So the strongest retention evidence may argue for the OPPOSITE of an AI-software-only surface — and there is no evidence isolating the AI layer's contribution. For the build/no-build call, this is the weakest link.

VOICE/TALK-VS-TYPE IN ONCOLOGY SPECIFICALLY: 'Almost no head-to-head adherence/engagement data exists for VOICE check-ins vs typed/tapped forms in oncology.' The only on-point voice-symptom test FAILED, and the only adherence numbers are from n=5-15 elderly-pain feasibility studies. If the daily companion's differentiator is conversational/voice input, the evidence base for that modality in this population is near-empty and what exists is negative.

DUTCH-PATIENT-SPEECH-TO-SYMPTOM PIPELINE END-TO-END: 'No found study tested LLM symptom/mood extraction from patient natural SPEECH in DUTCH.' The Dutch evidence is ASR-error-rate only; the symptom-extraction evidence is all English clinical TEXT. The combined pipeline for the actual home market is completely unvalidated — a build risk with zero direct evidence either way.

MONTH-3+ INDIVIDUAL RETENTION FOR A SOFTWARE-ONLY DAILY CHECK-IN: 'No source gave a clean, isolated month-3 individual retention number for a software-only daily check-in.' The month-3-cliff guidance and the streak-backfire constraint both rest on a single practitioner blog with no methodology. The two findings most likely to shape the retention model and the gamification design are the two with the weakest sourcing.

NL/EU AI DAILY-HEALTH-COMPANION RETENTION (any condition): 'No NL/EU-specific AI daily-health-companion retention data was found' — Limbic (UK/NHS) is the closest. Consumer-pay daily-habit benchmarks in the EU are thin; almost all disclosures are US employer/payer-sponsored programs where the user didn't pay and had external incentive, which inflates engagement vs a consumer-pay Dutch product. The retention assumptions are being imported across both disease AND market boundaries.

DOES VOICE/ACOUSTIC BIOMARKER SURVIVE AT ALL: The category leader Kintsugi SHUT DOWN (Feb 2026) with marginal independent validation (71.3% sensitivity, severe gender bias), and field-wide only 1 of 89 / 1 of 308 models reached clinical-implementation consideration. If any part of the proposed companion leans on passive acoustic mood/symptom sensing, the evidence base is not just thin — it is actively a graveyard, and that should be weighed against the build case directly.
